BOARD OF SUPERVISORS:
 
a. Consideration and acceptance of the resignation of Pamela Phillips as the
Public Fiduciary Director and appointment of Eileen Rogers as the new
Public Fiduciary Director, effective 7/1/2025 :
Pamela Phillips expressed sincere gratitude to the board for the
opportunity to serve as the Navajo County Public Fiduciary over the past
three and a half years. She spoke about the honor and privilege of the
role, especially given the importance of the work and the vulnerable
population they serve, which are often individuals who have no one else to
help them. She thanked Bryan Layton, HR, Administration, and Jayson
Vowell for their support and guidance during a time of significant transition,
acknowledging how much that help meant during an initially overwhelming
period.  She introduced Eileen Rogers, praising her as an essential part of
the team and someone without whom the job could not have been done.
She stated that Ms. Rogers has worked for the county for over 30 years
and over 20 years in the department, noting that her experience,
knowledge, compassion, and empathy make her exceptionally qualified for
the role. She recommended that the Board accept her resignation and
appoint Eileen Rogers as the next Public Fiduciary.
Eileen Rogers expressed gratitude for Ms. Phillip’s leadership, describing
her as a great boss and role model. She requested consideration to be
  
                                                                    2 of 13 
DRAFT

<!-- page 8 -->
appointed as the next Public Fiduciary, highlighting 22 years of service in
the office. She spoke of the continuous learning that comes from the job,
conferences, and even clients. She indicated that, while excited to take the
next step, she will miss the people she currently serves.
Vice-Chair Whitesinger expressed deep gratitude to Ms. Phillips for her
19 years of dedicated service, praising her compassion and the unique
impact of her department. She spoke of the lasting legacy she leaves
behind and extended her best wishes to Ms. Rogers, recognizing the
special commitment required to serve in such a role.
Supervisor Whitesinger made a motion to accept the resignation of
Pamela Phillips as the Public Fiduciary Director and appoint Eileen Rogers
as the new Public Fiduciary Director, effective 7/1/2025, motion seconded
by Supervisor Benally.
Chairman Whiting thanked both individuals for their service to Navajo
County.  He wished Ms. Phillips well in the next chapter of her life, and
acknowledged the servant's heart required for the role, expressing deep
appreciation for how well she fulfilled it.
Vote unanimous approving the motion.

NORTHEASTERN ARIZONA INNOVATIVE WORKFORCE SOLUTIONS: 
 
a. Consideration of award of Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act
(WIOA) One-Stop Operator, Contract B25-04-003 to Head Forward
Solutions LLC: 
Adam Garrard spoke about issues with the continued lack of the One Stop
Operator reauthorization since its expiration in 2016, resulting in annual
budget reductions of up to 18%. He indicated that to address these
funding constraints, the department is pursuing more cost-effective and
innovative contract solutions. He stated that this contract would offer a
lower cost than the previous $140,000 agreement, and that the selected
contractor is experienced, having served as the current one-stop operator
and now operating under an LOC.  He indicated that this contract and
related efforts are part of a broader initiative to strengthen compliance and
address prior audit findings, ensuring the department remains on track
both operationally and financially.
Chairman Whiting thanked Mr. Garrad for his leadership, as well as
looking for solutions.
Vice-Chair Whitesinger made a motion to approve the award of
Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) One-Stop Operator,
Contract B25-04-003 to Head Forward Solutions LLC, motion seconded
by Supervisor Benally.  Motion passed 4-0, with Supervisor Peshlakai
being absent for the vote.

WORK SESSION: 
The Work Session was called to order at 10:08 a.m.
 
a. Budget Presentation:
Bryan Layton emphasized the importance of transparency and public
engagement in public works initiatives. He indicated that the county wants
to not only implement great programs based on data but also share those
programs with the public in a clear, open manner. He further indicated that
Madhav Mundle will share information and ways of communicating public
works efforts to the communities.
Madhav Mundle provided an overview of the Capital Improvement
Program (CIP) and highway maintenance. He explained that the CIP is a
five-year plan covering 2026 to 2030, with funding from various grants like
RAISE, E-Z Smart, and potentially an OSB grant. He spoke about highway
maintenance, focusing on transparency and public information. He further
spoke about a new feature on the Public Works website: gravel road
maintenance reports, noting that the reports provide detailed information
about road maintenance, including current and previous quarterly reports,
specific details of road grading, location and length of roadways and
district-specific information.  Mr. Mundle highlighted that more than 45% of
their roads are gravel roads and that they try to maintain these roads every
eight weeks. He indicated that the reports allow residents to easily search
and find when and where their specific roads were graded. He noted that
the goal is to make this information readily accessible to the public, helping
residents understand the county's road maintenance efforts.
Chairman Whiting acknowledged the efforts of Mr. Mundle in making
road maintenance information transparent and accessible. He shared his
appreciation to the department for responding to board members' requests
by providing detailed road maintenance reports, noting that these reports
can help address common inquiries from residents, such as distinguishing
  
                                                                    6 of 13 
DRAFT

<!-- page 12 -->
between county and private roads. He requested clarification about the
road maintenance frequency.
Mr. Mundle confirmed that unpaved roads are graded approximately every
eight weeks, with current and previous quarterly reports available to help
residents track maintenance activities.
Mr. Mundle discussed gravel road stabilization. He explained that over
45% of their roads are gravel roads, including forest service, primitive, and
regular gravel roads. He indicated that they currently maintain roads by
spraying water and using motor graders every eight weeks, often ahead of
schedule. He further indicated that the county is experimenting with road
stabilization techniques to reduce dust and improve road durability, noting
that they are testing different admixtures and materials to find solutions
that work with their varied soil conditions. He stated that their approach
involves selecting one subdivision every alternate year for stabilization,
conducting pilot projects in different districts, trying new materials to
improve road conditions and maintaining routine maintenance alongside
stabilization efforts.  He indicated that previous pilot projects have yielded
mixed results, however, they continue to research and test methods to find
the most effective stabilization technique for their diverse county terrain.
Mr. Layton spoke about the gravel road stabilization efforts, explaining that
paving these roads would be extremely expensive, as it requires
comprehensive road design, drainage considerations, and significant
infrastructure changes.  He indicated that they are trying innovative,
low-cost techniques to make gravel roads more passable and reduce
maintenance needs. Mr. Layton noted that they are experimenting with
organic materials like tree saps and other techniques proven in other
areas, however, Navajo County's unique challenges include diverse soil
types and varying temperatures across different districts, which means
solutions that work in one area may not work in another. He indicated that
the goal is to find cost-effective ways to improve road conditions without
the massive expense of full paving.
Chairman Whiting reviewed the maintenance approach for gravel vs.
paved roads, noting that it is his understanding that one approach is
ongoing routine maintenance, while the other is a proactive effort to
improve and stabilize road conditions over time. 
Supervisor Benally inquired if gravel road stabilization is more than
putting gravel down.
Mr. Mundle provided additional information regarding the gravel road
stabilization project, indicating that the process involves more than just
adding gravel, it includes adding extra admixtures and chemicals, blending
them into the road, and compacting the surface. He stated that the goal is
to create a more durable road that remains stable for a longer period and
potentially reduces maintenance cycles. Mr. Mundle spoke about the
cost-effectiveness of this approach, noting that it costs only 1-5% of what it
would take to construct a brand-new roadway, which is significantly
cheaper because building a new road involves extensive and expensive
processes like widening rights-of-way, addressing drainage issues, adding
striping and signage, and potentially replacing sub-grade materials. He
noted they have selected 8-9 subdivisions, with plans to stabilize 4-5 this
year and the rest next year. He indicated that these efforts are focused
only on unincorporated areas, and the project aims to improve road

conditions while keeping costs minimal.
Supervisor Seymore shared concerns about road maintenance,
emphasizing the need to consider increased traffic flow in various areas.
He indicated that some roads may require more frequent grading due to
higher traffic volumes, such as Burton Road, noting how a road that was
once in excellent condition has deteriorated to a washboard-like state. He
recommended not just focusing on admixtures, but also potentially redoing
the road base, suggesting basalt base as a good mixture that holds up well
in most terrains. He indicated that they should always be looking at ways
to improve and maintain roads, especially in high-traffic areas.
Mr. Mundle explained that their stabilization plan involves not just adding
admixtures, but also blending and compacting the base, noting that their
goal is to create a more durable road surface that can withstand heavier
traffic and potential speeding. He indicated that by improving the road's
base and using stabilization techniques, they hope to reduce road damage
even when drivers exceed the posted 25 mph speed limit. He stated that
the aim is to create a road surface that can sustain heavy traffic and
remain more resilient to wear and tear.
Supervisor Benally shared her experience with road stabilization,
specifically referencing a project on Highway 41. She indicated that while
the initial road treatment was perfect for about two to three years, it
eventually broke down noting that the treated areas returned to their
original clay surface, and that she believes the method might work better
for slower traffic but is less effective on a major road like Highway 41
through the Black Mesa region.
Mr. Mundle indicated that if the road stabilization method lasted for two to
three years, it would be considered successful. He stated this as a positive
outcome, which is why they plan to continue the stabilization project every
other year, learning and improving from each attempt.
Supervisor Benally asked about road maintenance for stabilized roads,
specifically inquiring if maintenance would be similar to paved roads, such
as fixing potholes in the same manner, but using different materials. She
inquired how much wash boarding is expected.
Mr. Mundle indicated that when a stabilized road develops potholes or
wash boarding, they would send a motor grader to smooth out the surface
and fix the issues, similar to their current maintenance approach for gravel
roads. He further indicated that if drivers follow the speed limit, they
shouldn't experience much wash boarding. He noted that on primitive
roads, where they have less control over road conditions, high-speed
driving can quickly cause the road surface to deteriorate, and it’s best for
drivers to maintain a lower speed to preserve the road's condition.  Mr.
Mundle spoke about the Pavement Management Program, indicating that
the county hired a consultant to collect data on road conditions using a
laser-guided van to assess distress, potholes, and cracking. He stated that
the consultant generated a Pavement Condition Index (PCI) for each
road, and that while many agencies stop at generating this index, Navajo
County went a step further and created a comprehensive 10-year
Pavement Preservation Plan, which includes detailed cost estimates for
road treatments, specific streets and recommended treatments,
inflation-adjusted costs and a strategic approach to road maintenance.  He
indicated that maintaining all roads in fair to good condition would require
                                                                    8 of 13 
DRAFT

<!-- page 14 -->
$4 million annually, however, the county only has $2 million available for
road preservation, so they've strategically selected projects worth $2
million for the first year, focusing on slurry seal treatments and prioritizing
roads based on their condition and available budget. Mr. Mundle spoke
about the importance of using data-driven decision-making to manage
road maintenance efficiently within budget constraints.
Chairman Whiting spoke about the need for better state-level funding for
road maintenance. He emphasized that the current gas tax system,
created in 1985, is no longer sufficient to maintain roads. He noted that
Arizona's roads are deteriorating due to inadequate funding and suggested
that the state needs to find a new funding mechanism that accounts for
changes like electric vehicles, which don't contribute to the traditional gas
tax.
Mr. Layton noted that while they can empathize with the funding issue,
they now have clear data to demonstrate the specific funding gap in
Navajo County and indicated that by presenting concrete numbers and
analysis, they can speak credibly about the road maintenance shortfall and
the need for additional funding. He suggested using this data-driven
approach to engage with the state and potentially develop more effective
funding solutions for road infrastructure.
Mr. Mundle spoke about the need for around $4 million annually to
maintain roads properly. He explained that if they don't address road
maintenance each year, the costs will continue to increase due to inflation
and that to keep the 10-year plan manageable, they've aimed to keep the
annual cost around $4 million, adjusting for inflation. He indicated that this
allows them to create a reasonable long-term road maintenance strategy
within their financial constraints.
Mr. Layton spoke about discussing potential priorities at the County
Managers Association meeting. He suggested that if the board has a
strong sentiment about road funding or infrastructure challenges, he can
bring those concerns to the meeting to help staff understand what
research and work they should prioritize based on board input.
Mr. Mundle discussed the fiscal year 2026 pavement preservation project.
He highlighted a specific project in the Heber subdivision involving slurry
seal work on High Country Pines. He indicated that while this is just one
example for the current fiscal year, they plan to add more projects, noting
that the long-term goal is to eventually integrate these projects into a GIS
platform, allowing real-time public access to information about road
maintenance. He indicated that this would include details like when and
where maintenance was performed, creating a transparent and interactive
way for residents to track road improvement efforts.
Rochelle Lacapa provided an overview of the transportation infrastructure
funding challenges in Arizona. She indicated that the data shows that
purchasing power for highway user funds has decreased by 67%, vehicle
license tax has exceeded gas tax for the first time, the number of poor
roads in Arizona is increasing, and ADOT estimates a $112 million shortfall
for infrastructure.  She outlined potential tools available to the legislature
and counties for financing road improvements, including gas and fuel tax,
which requires a super majority vote; increasing vehicle license tax;
creating alternate fuel tax parity; county road excise tax; regional
transportation excise tax and road improvement districts.  She noted that
                                                                    9 of 13 
DRAFT

<!-- page 15 -->
while the Arizona County Supervisors Association has a policy resolution
supporting infrastructure investment, they are not running specific bills.
She suggests that Navajo County could potentially take the lead in
proposing a bill through CSA, emphasizing the need for increased funding
to address road maintenance challenges.
Supervisor Seymore inquired about the potential costs of putting a county
road excise tax to a vote. He indicated that the state may not address the
road maintenance problem soon and suggested exploring a local option
where Navajo County residents could vote on a dedicated road tax. He
inquired about the initial costs and feasibility of putting such a referendum
on the ballot.
A discussion was held about potential funding solutions for road
maintenance.  Ms. Lacapa explains the challenges of implementing a
county road excise tax, noting the current jail district tax generates $6
million annually. Mr. Layton suggested the campaign costs could be
several thousand dollars. Supervisor Seymore proposed exploring a
county road excise tax and potentially collaborating with cities and towns to
address road maintenance shortfalls. Supervisor Whitesinger indicated
that she agreed with Supervisor Seymore, recognizing the ongoing
challenges with state funding. She asked about the super majority
requirement and potential strategies for changing voting thresholds. Ms.
Lacapa explained the super majority rules and suggested that lowering the
threshold might face significant push backs from tax-averse groups. Mr.
Layton reviewed the board's comments about exploring state-level funding
solutions, investigating local funding options, considering polling to
understand public sentiment and potentially engage with local townships
and communities and ask for staff to gather more information about
potential funding mechanisms, explore polling to understand the public’s
position for a road tax, and to continue discussions about addressing road
maintenance funding gaps.
A presentation was shown.  Mr. Layton discussed the budget, highlighting
how the county has worked to improve employee compensation since
2016, including implementing consistent cost of living adjustments,
creating longevity adjustments, redesigning pay ranges to be
market-comparable, developing progression plans for career development,
and establishing anniversary step increases to help employees move up
pay ranges.  He spoke about how employee pay distribution has improved,
with a more natural spread across pay ranges. He discussed the current
budget constraints and proposed a modest cost of living adjustment,
discontinuing anniversary step increases, focusing on merit-based pay,
and introducing a new sabbatical program for long-term employees.  He
indicated that the sabbatical program would offer 2 days off at 5 years, 1
week at 10 years and 2 weeks at 15 years, with the option to sell back
time, noting that the time would have to be used consecutively within a
12-month period. He further indicated that the goal is to provide employees
with an opportunity to create meaningful experiences, give them resources
to potentially travel or do something special, recognize and appreciate
long-term service and create an emotional connection between employees
and the county.  He emphasized that this is a low-cost initiative with
potentially high emotional impact and that they hope employees will
remember the experience and appreciate the county's support.
                                                                    10 of 13 
DRAFT

<!-- page 16 -->
Mr. Scott shared an experience about an employee who worked in the
Public Works Road Yard for 30 years and their comment about how the
county has significantly improved its recognition program, taking employee
appreciation to a new level. He spoke about the positive impact of the
county's evolving approach to recognizing and valuing long-term
employees.
A discussion was held regarding the timeline for using the sabbatical time. 
Mr. Layton indicated that the goal is to encourage employees to actually
use their time off, rather than accumulating unused vacation, noting that
employees would work with their supervisors to plan and schedule their
sabbatical time within the 12-month window.
Mr. Layton discussed the county's vehicle and capital spending strategy. 
He indicated as to the vehicle fleet that Sheriff's patrol vehicles are
replaced at 160,000 miles and patrol vehicles cost around $70-80,000
each.  He further indicated that the goal is to replace 10 vehicles annually
to maintain low mileage and that the volunteer vehicles are repurposed
older patrol cars.  He spoke about the IT Infrastructure, noting that
computers are replaced every four years which is a centralized
replacement strategy, that the servers and network software remain
expensive and that cloud migration ongoing.  He further spoke about
building upgrades, including upgrading the door and camera security
systems, planning bathroom remodels, and preparing to repurpose Taylor
building space.  He indicated that upcoming major projects include a full
roof replacement which is estimated at $5 million, an HVAC system
overhaul and replacing outdated control boards and systems.  He indicated
that the total capital spending is estimated at approximately $3.4 million,
with funds allocated for unexpected repairs and replacements,
emphasizing being frugal while preventing infrastructure deterioration.
Jayson Vowell discussed the treasurer system replacement project, which
has been budgeted and delayed multiple times. He explained that some
projects like the treasurer system, facility upgrades, and fire alarm system
have been held over from previous years. 
Mr. Layton discussed healthcare costs and the county's successful
management strategy. He indicated that key points include healthcare
inflation, noting that national healthcare inflation is 7% this year, which is a
22% increase over past five years, that Navajo County's inflation has been
0-2% and that employee premiums have remained flat for nine years.  He
stated that successful strategies include encouraging use of Health Guide
services, negotiating cash prices with providers, connecting employees to
primary care, providing specialized health programs, and offering quick
payment to providers.  He spoke about the
Incentives, which include $500 added to HSA for employees getting an
annual physical and $300 added for the spouse's physical, noting that the
goal is to encourage preventive healthcare and that the current
participation is around 52% of employees.  He indicated that the approach
focuses on investing in employee health early to reduce long-term
healthcare costs and improve overall employee well-being.
Mr. Scott shared a story about an employee who got a physical primarily to
receive the HSA incentive and that during this physical, the doctor
discovered a significant medical concern that the employee believes could
have saved their life. He indicated that this is not an isolated incident and
                                                                    11 of 13 
DRAFT

<!-- page 17 -->
highlighted the importance of the county's health incentive program in
potentially catching serious health issues early.
Mr. Layton stated that the current annual physical participation rate is
52%.  He indicated that to increase participation they would propose
maintaining current HSA contributions, adding a $500 one-time cash
payment for employees getting physicals and an additional $300 if spouse
also gets a physical, noting that they goal is to increase participation to
60-70%.   
Chairman Whiting shared his appreciation for the incentive approach.
Supervisor Seymore highlighted how the HSA helps employees manage
their health deductible.
Ms. Lacapa spoke about the challenge of finding primary care providers.
Mr. Layton and Mr. Scott discussed partnering with the Public Health
Department to provide on-site wellness checks and potentially establish an
employee clinic day, addressing the shortage of primary care providers,
noting the importance of preventive healthcare and finding innovative ways
to support employee health.
Mr. Scott discussed law enforcement stress management and mental
health, noting that the previously implemented counseling for detectives
based on the Craig Tiger Act and sending detectives to the valley for
mandatory annual counseling. Mr. Layton indicated that moving forward
they will have a licensed counselor, Kimberly O'Farrell, on staff to provide
support and that they will expand counseling to include all deputies and
animal care officers.  He spoke about the program goals which include
helping employees manage emotional stress, developing strategies for
handling trauma, maintaining positive relationships in and out of work and
providing proactive mental health support.  He further spoke about the
communication strategy which includes conducting face-to-face meetings
with staff, using internal communication channels, conducting outreach to
explain new programs and ensuring employees understand available
support services. 
Chairman Whiting emphasized the importance of proactive
communication and continuous improvement in sharing information with
employees.
Mr. Layton discussed recommended improvements and budget proposals,
including staffing and position recommendations for a new custodial
position for the Taylor building, a Recorder's office salary adjustments to
align with market rates, the Treasurer's office getting a Loomis cash
recycler for improved cash handling, Security Operations Center support,
and two new administrator positions in the Sheriff's office.  He further
spoke about the key benefits of the recommendations which include
improved cash handling security, enhanced management capacity in
Sheriff's office, addressing specific departmental needs and maintaining
competitive salary structures.  Mr. Layton emphasized these
recommendations are carefully considered to support departmental
efficiency and employee needs while maintaining fiscal responsibility.
Mr. Vowell provided a budget overview, noting that FY 2025 was $45.3
million in revenues and expenditures and that FY2026 has a projected
increase to $46.5 million, with a potential revenue increase to $47.7
million.  He spoke about budget adjustments, noting that a 2.5%
across-the-board adjustment would cost $570,000, which includes funding
                                                                    12 of 13 
DRAFT

<!-- page 18 -->
for the custodial positions, salary adjustments and departmental needs. 
He further spoke about funding considerations which include three primary
revenue sources: property tax, county sales tax, state shared sales tax,
noting that the current property tax rate is third lowest in state and the
potential property tax increase could generate $218,000-$500,000.  He
emphasized the need to balance budget constraints with departmental
needs and focus on maintaining a fiscally responsible approach while
supporting county operations.
Mr. Layton stated that they plan to propose the budget on July 15, 2025,
and adopt the budget in August. He asked if the Board had feedback
regarding whether they are going in the right direction and if there are any
suggestions or adjustments they would like to see before the formal
budget proposal.
Vice-Chair Whitesinger shared her appreciation of the budget
preparation not just focusing on the current year, but also taking into
consideration future implications. She commended the approach of being
transparent with departments about budget constraints and emphasized
the importance of protecting employees and maintaining service quality.
She indicated that she values the organization's integrity and commitment
to investing in employees while maintaining professional service
standards.
Mr. Vowell emphasized that their fiscal planning is not just about FY2026
but about positioning the county for financial stability in future years
(2027-2029), noting that the goal is to make prudent decisions now that will
provide a solid financial foundation for the coming years, avoiding the need
to make drastic adjustments or cutbacks later.
Supervisor Seymore thanked the team for their work on the budget. He
acknowledged the potential for lean years ahead but indicated that he
feels confident in the county's capacity to adjust. He shared his
appreciation for the approach of valuing employees not just through pay,
but through comprehensive support like healthcare and career
development opportunities.
The Work Session ended at 12:11 p.m.

Department: Public Works
Motion before the Board:
Name an existing unnamed road in the Clay Springs area of Navajo County, to "Moonstone Lane",
located in Section 15, Township 11 North, Range 19 East
Background:
The District IV road is located within Section 15, Township 11 North, Range 19 East.
Easement: It was granted per Survey 2025-00379  on Map 5-9.
Please refer to the attached items for more details.
Purpose of Naming: To effectively address the needs of Emergency Services/E911, an access road needs a name
when three or more property owners use the same access. This road currently serves seven properties.
Road Name: Moonstone Lane was the name selected by the property owners. All property owners (the same two
individuals ) have been notified and have signed petitions accepting the road name.
This is not a county-maintained road.

Meeting Date: 06/24/2025  
Title: FY26 ACJC Drug, Gang, and Violent Crime Control (DGVCC) Grant Agreement
#DC-26-029
Submitted For: Brad Carlyon, County Attorney  Submitted By: Lynda Young, Office Manager
Department: County Attorney
Motion before the Board:
Acceptance of the FY26 ACJC Drug, Gang and Violent Crime Control (DGVCC) Grant Award
#DC-26-029 to pay partial salaries for two dedicated prosecutors to prosecute drug sales and trafficking
offenses
Background:
Through the Byrne grant, we are able to have dedicated attorneys that punish offenders of drug trafficking
in Navajo County. This grant, funded through the Arizona Criminal Justice Commission, allows our
attorneys to work closely with law enforcement, strengthening collaborations with other agencies,
resulting in stronger investigations. We expect to deprive these dealers and manufacturers from profits
through seizures and forfeitures. These efforts will slow down the drug operations in our county that
impact drug-related robbery and theft, drug-related domestic violence, drug-related child abuse, drugs
ripping apart families, and drugs invading our schools. 
Fiscal Impact
Fiscal Year: FY26
Budgeted Y/N: Y
Amount Requested: $227,435.1
Fiscal Impact:
Grant will fund $101,414.53 in salaries and $34,060.26 in fringe benefits.

33. The parties agree to use arbitration in the event of disputes in accordance with the provisions of A.R.S. §
12-1501-12-1518. The laws of the State of Arizona apply to questions arising under this Agreement and any
litigation regarding this Agreement must be maintained in Arizona courts, except as pertaining to disputes
which are subject to arbitration.
I. In the event of a dispute, controversy, or claim arising out of or relating in any way to the Agreement, the
complaining Party shall notify the other Party in writing thereof. Within 30 calendar days of such notice,
representatives of both Parties shall meet at an agreed location to attempt to resolve the dispute in good
faith. Should the dispute not be resolved within 30 calendar days after such notice, the complaining Party
shall seek remedies exclusively through arbitration, in accordance with the provisions of A.R.S. § 12-1501
through 12-1518.
II. The arbitration demand must be a clear and concise statement of the claim or dispute. The respondent's
answer and any counterclaims must be filed within 20 calendar days of service of the demand.
III. The arbitration shall be conducted in Maricopa County.
IV. The arbitration shall be conducted by one arbitrator. If the Parties are not able to agree upon the selection
of an arbitrator, within 20 calendar days of the commencement of an arbitration proceeding by service of a
demand for arbitration, the court on application of a Party shall appoint the arbitrator.

challenging the award.

From time to time, Arizona Criminal Justice Commission (we, us or Company) may be required 
by law to provide to you certain written notices or disclosures. Described below are the terms 
and conditions for providing to you such notices and disclosures electronically through the 
DocuSign system. Please read the information below carefully and thoroughly, and if you can

Signature Disclosure (ERSD), please confirm your agreement by selecting the check-box next to 
‘I agree to use electronic records and signatures’ before clicking ‘CONTINUE’ within the 
DocuSign system. 
 
Getting paper copies  
At any time, you may request from us a paper copy of any record provided or made available 
electronically to you by us. You will have the ability to download and print documents we send 
to you through the DocuSign system during and immediately after the signing session and, if you 
elect to create a DocuSign account, you may access the documents for a limited period of time 
(usually 30 days) after such documents are first sent to you. After such time, if you wish for us to 
send you paper copies of any such documents from our office to you, you will be charged a 
$0.00 per-page fee. You may request delivery of such paper copies from us by following the 
procedure described below. 
 
Withdrawing your consent  
If you decide to receive notices and disclosures from us electronically, you may at any time 
change your mind and tell us that thereafter you want to receive required notices and disclosures 
only in paper format. How you must inform us of your decision to receive future notices and 
disclosure in paper format and withdraw your consent to receive notices and disclosures 
electronically is described below. 
 
Consequences of changing your mind  
If you elect to receive required notices and disclosures only in paper format, it will slow the 
speed at which we can complete certain steps in transactions with you and delivering services to 
you because we will need first to send the required notices or disclosures to you in paper format, 
and then wait until we receive back from you your acknowledgment of your receipt of such 
paper notices or disclosures. Further, you will no longer be able to use the DocuSign system to 
receive required notices and consents electronically from us or to sign electronically documents 
from us. 
 
All notices and disclosures will be sent to you electronically

RESOLUTION NUMBER ____-2025
A RESOLUTION OF THE BOARD OF SUPERVISORS OF NAVAJO COUNTY
APPROVING THE FORM AND AUTHORIZING THE EXECUTION AND DELIVERY
OF AN AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE TREASURER OF NAVAJO COUNTY AND
WELLS FARGO BANK, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION PROVIDING FOR A LINE OF
CREDIT FOR NAVAJO COUNTY; RATIFYING ALL ACTIONS TAKEN TO DATE
WITH RESPECT TO SUCH AGREEMENTS.
RECITALS
WHEREAS, Wells Fargo Bank, National Association (the "Bank") entered into a Master
Banking Services Agreement dated June 7, 2023, with Graham County ("Graham County") under
which the Bank agreed to provide certain banking services (such contract being the "Graham
County Contract") and pursuant to the Graham County Contract, other governmental entities that
are members of the Strategic Alliance for Volume Expenditures ("SAVE") purchasing group or that
enter into intergovernmental cooperative purchasing agreements (each an "ICPA") with Graham
County are entitled to procure some or all of the banking services under the Graham County
Contract;
WHEREAS, Navajo County (the "County") is either a member of SAVE or has entered into
an ICPA and therefore is entitled to procure banking services from the Bank; and
WHEREAS, the Bank has agreed to provide certain banking services to the County as
specified in and subject to the terms and provisions of that certain Agreement for Banking Services
dated April 22, 2025, between the County and the Bank (such contract being the "Navajo County
Contract"), for the period commencing July 1, 2025 and ending June 30, 2026, with permitted
extensions pursuant to A.R.S. § 35-325; and
WHEREAS, one of the banking services the Bank is willing to provide pursuant to the
Navajo County Contract is a line of credit for the County pursuant to A.R.S § 11-604.01; and

<!-- page 94 -->
2
WHEREAS, A.R.S. §§ 11-604.01 et. seq., authorizes the Supervisors of the County to enter
into a line of credit agreement on behalf of the County; and
WHEREAS, a draft of the Business Loan Agreement (Navajo County Revolving Line of
Credit) providing a line of credit for the County and to be evidenced by a promissory note has been
provided by the Bank (upon execution and inclusive of the referenced promissory note, the
“County Agreement”) and has been placed on file with the Clerk of this Board and presented at the
meeting at which this Resolution was adopted; and
WHEREAS, by this Resolution the Supervisors will authorize the execution and delivery
of the County Agreement, in substantially the form so presented to the Board of Supervisors,
subject to the approval of the Navajo County Attorney.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE BOARD OF SUPERVISORS OF
NAVAJO COUNTY, as follows:
Section 1.  That a draft of the County Agreement, in substantially the form on file with the
Clerk, is approved and the Chairman of this Board (or any acting Chair of this Board) and the
Treasurer of the County are authorized and directed to execute and deliver the County Agreement
on file with the Clerk.
Section 2.  The County Treasurer is named as the County’s agent for all purposes of the
County Agreement.  The County Treasurer is authorized to take all acts and to do all things on
behalf of the County, including, with limitation, requesting amendments to the Commitment
Amount Cap under the County Agreement, provided that the Commitment Amount Cap shall not
be increased to an amount which exceeds $2,500,000.
Section 3 . All actions taken by the County Treasurer and any person representing the
County Treasurer with respect to the County Agreement, and the procedures pertaining thereto, are
hereby ratified and affirmed.  This Resolution shall become effective immediately upon adoption
and execution.

4931-2853-7669.1  
BUSINESS LOAN AGREEMENT 
(NAVAJO COUNTY REVOLVING LINE OF CREDIT) 
DATE: July 1, 2025 
PARTIES: County: Navajo County Board of Supervisors for Navajo 
County, through the Navajo County Treasurer, as its 
agent 
Bank: Wells Fargo Bank, National Association, a national 
banking association, authorized to do business in the 
State of Arizona (“Bank”) 
AGREEMENT:  Pursuant to Arizona Revised Statutes Sections 11-604.01 et. seq., (together with 
all amendments and statutes successor thereto, collectively, the “Act”), the Board of Supervisors 
of a county may enter into an agreement with the financial institution authorized to do business in 
the State of Arizona for the purpose of obtaining a line of credit for the County (as defined below).  
The Act further provides that the Navajo County Treasurer is the agent for the County and for each 
political subdivision of the State of Arizona for which the Navajo County Treasurer acts as 
treasurer and may take any action required under an agreement without further approval of any 
governing body of a political subdivision.  The Board of Supervisors of Navajo County 
(“County”), the Navajo County Treasurer and Bank intend to enter into this Agreement and the 
hereafter-described Note to obtain a line of credit pursuant to the Act for County, in the maximum 
amount of the Commitment Amount Cap (as defined herein), and to evidence such line of credit 
in this Agreement and the Note. For purposes of this Agreement and the line of credit extended to 
County evidenced hereunder and in the Note, County shall be acting through the Navajo County 
Treasurer as its agent pursuant to the Act.  For good and valuable consideration, the receipt and 
sufficiency of which are hereby acknowledged, County and Bank agree as follows: 
1. DEFINITIONS.  In this Agreement, the following terms shall have the following 
meanings: 
“Advance” means a disbursement of funds by Bank to County pursuant to Section 2.1. 
“Agreement” means this Business Loan Agreement (Navajo County Revolving Line of 
Credit) as it may be amended, modified, extended, renewed, restated, or supplemented from time 
to time. 
“Anti-Corruption Laws” means: (a) the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act of 1977, as 
amended; (b) the U.K. Bribery Act 2010, as amended; and (c) any other anti-bribery or anti-
corruption laws, regulations or ordinances in any jurisdiction in which County is located or doing 
business.

<!-- page 97 -->
2 
4931-2853-7669.1  
“Anti-Money Laundering Laws” means applicable laws or regulations in any jurisdiction 
in which County is located or doing business that relates to money laundering, any predicate crime 
to money laundering, or any financial record keeping and reporting requirements related thereto. 
“Authorized Person” means the Navajo County Treasurer (the signature appearing on this 
Agreement is a true and genuine specimen signature of the Navajo County Treasurer) or any other 
person authorized to act for County hereunder as shown by a written statement signed by the 
Navajo County Treasurer and that also shows the specimen signature of such additional Authorized 
Person. 
“Bank Services Agreement” means the Agreement for Banking Services dated April 22, 
2025, between County and Bank, as the same may be amended, modified or supplemented from 
time to time. 
“Business Day” means a day of the year on which banks are not required or authorized to 
close in Phoenix, Arizona. 
“Collateral” means, collectively, the property, interests in property, and rights to property 
securing any or all Obligations from time to time, including without limitation, the security interest 
in the nonrestricted operating revenues received by the Navajo County Treasurer on behalf of 
County. 
“Commitment” means the agreement of Bank to make Advances as provided in this 
Agreement. 
“Commitment Amount” means the lesser of (i) the Commitment Amount Cap, as it may 
be amended from time to time, or (ii) the Statutory Approved Amount. 
“Commitment Amount Cap” means initially, the amount of One Million and No/100 
Dollars ($1,000,000.00) as such amount may be amended in accordance with this Agreement from 
time to time.  
“Default Rate” has the meaning specified in the Note. 
“Event of Default” has the meaning specified in the Note. 
“Governmental Authority” means any government, any court, and any agency, authority, 
body, bureau, department, or instrumentality of any government. 
“Loan Documents” means, collectively, this Agreement, the Note, the Bank Services 
Agreement and any other agreements, documents, and instruments from time to time evidencing, 
guarantying, securing, or otherwise relating to the Note, as they may be amended, modified, 
extended, renewed, restated, or supplemented from time to time. 
“Note” means the Promissory Note, dated of even date herewith, of County payable to 
Bank, as it may be amended, modified, extended, renewed, restated, or supplemented from time 
to time.

4931-2853-7669.1  
“Obligations” means the respective obligations of County under the Loan Documents. 
“Online Portal” has the meaning set forth in Section 2.2 hereof. 
“Patriot Act” means the Uniting and Strengthening America by Providing Appropriate 
Tools Required to Intercept and Obstruct Terrorism Act of 2001, Title III of Pub. L. 107 56 (signed 
into law October 26, 2001). 
“Person” means a natural person, a partnership, a joint venture, an unincorporated

“Sanction” or “Sanctions” means any and all economic or financial sanctions, sectoral 
sanctions, secondary sanctions, trade embargoes and restrictions and anti-terrorism laws imposed, 
administered or enforced from time to time by: (a) the United States of America, including those 
administered by the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), 
the U.S. Department of State, the U.S. Department of Commerce, or through any existing or future 
statute or Executive Order, (b) the United Nations Security Council, (c) the European Union, (d)

of Sanctions, including vessels and aircraft, that are designated under any Sanctions program. 
“Scheduled Commitment Expiration Date” means June 30, 2026, subject to earlier

 “Servicing Bank Term” means the period during which Bank provides services to County 
as servicing bank pursuant to the Bank Services Agreement with such term commencing July 1, 
2025 and ending June 30, 2026, subject to extensions of not more than two additional years. 
“Statutory Approved Amount” means the amount which is (i) no greater than the amount 
equal to forty-five percent (45%) of the total nonrestricted operating revenues received by County 
during the immediately preceding fiscal year or, (ii) if County has not received nonrestricted 
operating revenues during the immediately preceding fiscal year, no greater than the amount equal 
to forty-five percent (45%) of County’s estimated first year nonrestricted operating revenues. 
“Unmatured Event of Default” means any condition or event that with notice, passage of 
time, or both would be an Event of Default. 
“Vantage” has the meaning set forth in Section 2.2 hereof. 
2. REVOLVING LINE OF CREDIT FACILITY.

<!-- page 99 -->
4 
4931-2853-7669.1  
2.1 Credit Facility.  Subject to the terms and conditions of this Agreement, Bank 
agrees to make Advances to County from time to time on or before the Scheduled Commitment 
Expiration Date, provided that the outstanding amount of Advances shall not exceed the 
Commitment Amount.  Advances to County shall be on a revolving basis. Advances repaid may 
be re-borrowed, subject to the terms and conditions of this Agreement.  Upon occurrence of an 
Event of Default or an Unmatured Event of Default, Bank, in its absolute and sole discretion and 
without notice, may suspend the commitment to make Advances.  In addition, upon occurrence of 
an Event of Default, Bank, in its absolute and sole discretion and without notice, may terminate 
the commitment to make Advances.  The obligation of County to repay Advances is evidenced by 
the Note as to the amount outstanding thereunder.  Although the outstanding principal of the Note 
may be zero from time to time, the Loan Documents shall remain in full force and effect until the 
Commitment terminates and all Obligations are paid and performed in full. 
2.2 Requests for Advances and Repayments.  Each request for an Advance will 
be made in writing in a manner mutually acceptable to Bank and the Navajo County Treasurer, or 
by another means mutually acceptable to Bank and the Navajo County Treasurer.  For the 
avoidance of doubt, the Navajo County Treasurer may submit its request for an Advance through 
Bank’s Wells Fargo Vantage (“Vantage”) f/k/a Commercial Electronic Office (CEO) portal 
(Vantage, or any replacement or successor portal, the “Online Portal”). 
2.3 Advances and Repayments. 
Advances will be deposited in and repayments will be withdrawn from the designated 
account of County with Bank, initially being the account number ending in 1508, or such other 
accounts with Bank as designated in writing by an Authorized Person; provided that such deposits 
and repayments may be made by way of the Online Portal.  County hereby irrevocably authorizes 
and directs Bank to make such credits and debits in accordance with the terms of this Agreement.  
The arrangement in this Section 2.3 to debit such demand deposit account for any amounts due 
under the Loan Documents shall not restrict Bank’s right to collect any amounts due under the 
Loan Documents from any revenues or funds of County otherwise available for payment of such 
amounts, including, without limitation, all nonrestricted operating revenues of County. 
2.4 Advances - Repayment.  County agrees to apply all “nonrestricted operating 
revenues,” as such term is described in the Act according to the priorities set forth in the Act.  If 
there remain any amounts outstanding on the Note as of June 30 of any year, County agrees to 
notify Bank on or before June 30 of such year of the amounts on deposit in the demand deposit 
account and other accounts of County with Bank which constitute nonrestricted operating 
revenues. 
2.5 Advances in Excess of Commitment Amount.  If with or without the 
approval of Bank the aggregate outstanding amount of Advances to County at any time exceeds 
the Commitment Amount, County shall repay the excess immediately upon demand by Bank. 
2.6 Authority to Amend Commitment.  In accordance with the provisions of the 
Act, the Navajo County Treasurer on behalf of County is hereby authorized to request Bank to 
amend this Agreement and the Note from time to time with respect to the following matters:

<!-- page 100 -->
5 
4931-2853-7669.1  
2.6.1 To extend the Scheduled Commitment Expiration Date, as described 
in Section 2.8; and 
2.6.2 To increase or decrease the Commitment Amount Cap, provided 
that the Commitment Amount Cap shall not be increased to an amount which exceeds $2,500,000, 
without such amendment being approved by resolution adopted by the Navajo County Board of 
Supervisors; and 
2.6.3 County understands, acknowledges and agrees that any request of 
Bank pursuant to this Section 2.6 shall be decided by Bank (in each instance) acting in Bank’s sole 
and absolution discretion. 
2.7 Procedure to Amend Commitment.  The Agreement and Note may be 
amended by a written amendment substantially in the form attached hereto as Exhibit B (the 
“Addendum”) executed by Bank and by the Navajo County Treasurer on behalf of County.  Each 
amendment, when dated and fully executed, shall be construed to amend all prior versions of this 
Agreement and Note, whether or not it is actually attached to all copies of this Agreement or the 
Note. 
2.8 Extension of Scheduled Commitment Expiration Date.  The Commitment 
provided to County hereunder shall be in effect initially for fiscal year 2025-2026.  County and 
Bank (acting in its sole and absolute discretion) may agree to extend the Commitment for each 
fiscal year thereafter through the execution of the Addendum extending the Scheduled 
Commitment Expiration Date to June 30 of the next calendar year.  Notwithstanding the foregoing, 
nothing set forth herein authorizes the Commitment to be extended beyond the expiration of the 
Servicing Bank Term. 
3. CONDITIONS PRECEDENT TO ADVANCES. 
3.1 CONDITIONS PRECEDENT TO INITIAL ADVANCE.  Bank must 
receive the following items, in form and content acceptable to Bank, before Bank is required to 
make any Advances to County under this Agreement. 
3.1.1 Legal Opinion of County. A written opinion of the legal counsel for 
County, in a form satisfactory to Bank, opining on the following: 
(a) Authorization.  The execution, delivery, and performance by County of the 
Loan Documents have been duly authorized by all requisite action by or on behalf of 
County. 
(b) Enforceability.  The Loan Documents have been duly executed and 
delivered on behalf of County.  The Loan Documents are legal, valid, and binding 
obligations of County, enforceable in accordance with their terms against County, except 
as such enforceability may be limited by Arizona Revised Statutes Sections 42-17101 et. 
seq., bankruptcy, insolvency, moratorium, reorganization, or similar laws and by equitable 
principles of general application.

Note.  
3.1.3 County Resolution.  A copy of the resolution of the County 
approving this Agreement and the Note. 
3.1.4 County’s Financial Statement and Annual Budget.  A copy of 
County’s published annual financial statement for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024 (and Bank 
reserves the right to receive copies of (i) County’s financial statements for fiscal years thereafter 
and (ii) the adopted budget for County for each fiscal year) and such other information and 
documents as Bank may reasonably request.   
3.2 CONDITIONS PRECEDENT TO ALL ADVANCES.  Bank shall be 
obligated to make an Advance when requested on behalf of County only if the following conditions 
precedent are satisfied. 
3.2.1 Representations and Warranties Accurate.  The representations and 
warranties by County in the Loan Documents are correct on and as of the date of this Agreement 
and, except as County shall have otherwise notified Bank in writing prior to the date thereof, on 
and as of the date of each Advance, before and after giving effect to such Advance and to the 
application of the proceeds of such Advance, as though made on and as of such date. 
3.2.2 No Violation of Limits on Advances.  The making of the Advance 
to County would not result in the outstanding amount of Advances exceeding the Commitment 
Amount. 
3.2.3 No Material Adverse Change.  As of the date of an Advance, no 
material adverse change shall have occurred in the financial condition of County since the date of 
the most recent financial statements of County provided to Bank.  A “material adverse change” 
shall be deemed to have occurred when Bank provides notice that it has determined, based upon 
financial information provided to it by County or other information available to Bank that County 
is not reasonably likely to be capable of repaying the outstanding amount of Advances owed to 
Bank on or before the Scheduled Commitment Expiration Date.  
3.2.4 No Event of Default or Unmatured Event of Default.   As of the date 
of an Advance, no Event of Default or Unmatured Event of Default shall exist or result from the 
making of the Advance. 
3.3 Bank’s Waiver of Conditions.  Bank may elect, in its absolute and sole 
discretion, to waive any of the foregoing conditions precedent.  Any such waiver shall be effective 
only if (i) it is in writing executed by Bank, (ii) it specifically identifies the condition precedent, 
and (iii) describes the particular Advance as to which such condition precedent is waived.  Any 
such waiver shall be limited to the condition(s) precedent specifically described therein.  Delay or 
failure by Bank to insist on satisfaction of any condition precedent of an Advance shall not be a 
waiver of such condition precedent or any other condition precedent.  If County is unable to satisfy 
any condition precedent of an Advance, the making of the Advance shall not preclude Bank from 
thereafter declaring the condition or event causing such inability to be an Event of Default.

give representatives of Bank access to all assets, property, books, records, and documents of 
County and shall permit such representatives to inspect such assets and property and to audit, copy, 
examine, and make excerpts from such books, records, and documents. 
5.3 Information and Statements.  County shall furnish to Bank: (i) within thirty 
(30) days of their receipt, but in no event later than March 25 th of each year, copies of County’s 
audited financial statements for the immediately preceding fiscal year, together with any reports 
or comment letters of the auditor, (ii) within thirty (30) days after adoption, but in no event later

County’s budget is to be paid from moneys authorized to be collected pursuant to a budget override 
election, a copy of the election canvass certificate, (v) any other information and documents given

shall comply in all material respects with all material agreements, documents, and instruments to 
which County is a party or by which County or any of the assets or property of County is bound

Bank under the Loan Documents. 
5.6 Use of Advances.   
5.6.1 County shall use proceeds of Advances only to pay expenses 
incurred in its general operations (collectively, “Operating Expenses”) and shall be limited to the 
extent set forth in Section 4.1.8 hereof.  County shall only use proceeds of Advances to pay then 
due Operating Expenses, and shall only receive such Advances when it has no other available 
funds to pay such Operating Expenses.  County shall not use the Advances to purchase or carry 
margin stock (within the meaning of Regulation U of the Board of Governors of the Federal 
Reserve System) or to extend credit to others for the purpose of purchasing or carrying margin 
stock or to refund indebtedness originally incurred for such purpose, in each case in violation of, 
or for a purpose which violates, or would be inconsistent with, Regulation T, U or X of the Board 
of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. 
5.6.2 County shall not, directly or indirectly use any of the proceeds of 
Advances to fund, finance or facilitate any activities, business or transactions that would be 
prohibited by Anti-Money Laundering Laws or Anti-Corruption Laws. 
5.6.3 County shall not, directly or indirectly use any of the proceeds of 
Advances to fund, finance or facilitate any activities, business or transactions: (i) that are 
prohibited by Sanctions, (ii) that would be prohibited by U.S. Sanctions if conducted by a U.S. 
Person, or (iii) that would be prohibited by Sanctions if conducted by Bank, or any other party to

County, shall perform its obligations under the Act, including without limitation, under Arizona 
Revised Statutes Section 11-604.01.E thereof, which Act is hereby incorporated herein by 
reference. 
5.8 Security Interest Grants.  County shall not grant or suffer to exist any lien, 
claim, or encumbrance to or in favor of any person or entity other than Bank covering the 
nonrestricted operating revenues of County (it being understood that Tax Anticipation Notes, 
General Obligation Bonds, and other payment-source-specific financing commitments of County 
deal with operating revenues which are restricted and thus are not “nonrestricted operating 
revenues”).  County and Bank agree that Bank is entitled to a security interest in the nonrestricted 
operating revenues received by the Navajo County Treasurer on behalf of County to the extent of 
any credit extended under this Agreement. 
5.9 Policies and Procedures.  County shall maintain in effect policies and 
procedures that address matters relating to compliance by County and its directors, officers, 
employees and agents with Sanctions, Anti-Money Laundering Laws and Anti-Corruption Laws. 
5.10 Source of Repayment and Collateral.  County shall not fund any repayment 
of any Advance with proceeds, or provide as collateral any property, that is directly or indirectly 
derived from any transaction or activity that is prohibited by Sanctions, Anti-Money Laundering 
Laws or Anti-Corruption Laws, or that could otherwise cause Bank or any other party to this 
Agreement to be in violation of Sanctions, Anti-Money Laundering Laws or Anti-Corruption

2. INTEREST RATE. The Interest Rate (the “Interest Rate”) during each calendar 
quarter shall be the rate per annum equal to the rate per annum most recently publicly announced 
by Bank, or Bank’s successors, in Phoenix, Arizona, as Bank’s “prime rate”, as in effect from time 
to time, provided that in no event shall the Interest Rate at any time exceed one hundred ten percent 
(110%) of the previous quarter’s weighted average prime rate among the top three financial 
institutions by asset size in the State of Arizona.  The Interest Rate will be redetermined by Bank 
on each day that the “prime rate” changes and any changes in the Interest Rate will be effective on 
and after the date of such change and until the next change.  The “prime rate” is set by Bank based 
on various factors, including Bank’s costs and desired return, general economic conditions and 
other factors, and is used as a reference point in pricing some loans.  Bank may price loans to its 
customers at, above, or below its “prime rate.”  Notwithstanding the foregoing, in no event shall 
the Interest Rate at any time be less than zero percent (0.00%).

3. REQUIRED PAYMENTS; PAYMENT ON MATURITY.  Prior to June 30, 2026, 
or if the Scheduled Commitment Expiration Date under the Loan Agreement has been extended 
by mutual agreement between County, acting through its agent, the Navajo County Treasurer, and 
Bank (acting in its sole and absolute discretion), such Scheduled Commitment Expiration Date 
(the “Maturity Date”), payments under this Note shall be made as County receives “nonrestricted 
operating revenues”, as such term is used in the Act. On the Maturity Date, County shall pay to 
Bank the unpaid principal, all accrued and unpaid interest, and all other amounts (“Other 
Amounts”) payable by County to Bank under the Loan Documents (as defined in the Loan 
Agreement). 
4. INTEREST ON PRINCIPAL; DEFAULT RATE. Principal shall bear interest at 
the Interest Rate from the date of disbursement until the due date thereof, whether by acceleration 
or otherwise. Principal, interest, and Other Amounts not paid when due and any judgment therefor 
shall bear interest from its due date or the judgment date, as applicable, until paid at a rate (the 
“Default Rate”) per annum equal to one hundred ten percent (110.00%) of the previous quarter’s 
weighted average prime rate among the top three financial institutions by asset size in the State of 
Arizona (unless a lower maximum rate of interest is then applicable under the Act, in which case, 
the Default Rate shall be such lower rate of interest under the Act), and such interest shall be 
immediately due and payable. 
5. INTEREST ACCRUAL. All interest under the Loan Documents shall be computed 
on the basis of a 365-day year and accrue on a daily basis for the actual number of days elapsed. 
County agrees to pay an effective rate of interest that is the sum of (i) the Interest Rate and (ii) any 
additional rate of interest resulting from any other charges or fees paid or to be paid in connection 
herewith that are determined to be interest or in the nature of interest. 
6. PAYMENT IN FULL PRIOR TO THE MATURITY DATE. Notwithstanding any 
other provision herein or in the Loan Documents, County shall pay to Bank all outstanding 
principal, interest and Other Amounts on June 30 of each year. So long as County makes such 
payment, County shall, subject to the provisions of the Loan Agreement, continue to be entitled to 
Advances pursuant to the Loan Agreement prior to the commitment expiration date specified 
therein. Principal, interest, and Other Amounts not paid on June 30 of each year shall bear interest 
from June 30 until paid at the Default Rate, and such interest shall be immediately due and payable. 
7. APPLICATION OF PAYMENTS. At the option of Bank, payments shall be 
applied to principal, interest, and Other Amounts in such order as Bank shall determine. 
8. PREPAYMENT. County may prepay the outstanding principal balance hereof, in 
whole or in part, at any time prior to the Maturity Date without penalty or premium. 
9. NO COUNTERCLAIMS, DEDUCTIONS, ETC. All payments and other 
obligations of County under the Loan Documents will be made and performed without 
counterclaim, deduction, defense, deferment, reduction, or set-off.

of Default”):

2. INTEREST RATE. The Interest Rate (the “Interest Rate”) during each calendar 
quarter shall be the rate per annum equal to the rate per annum most recently publicly announced 
by Bank, or Bank’s successors, in Phoenix, Arizona, as Bank’s “prime rate”, as in effect from time 
to time, provided that in no event shall the Interest Rate at any time exceed one hundred ten percent 
(110%) of the previous quarter’s weighted average prime rate among the top three financial 
institutions by asset size in the State of Arizona.  The Interest Rate will be redetermined by Bank 
on each day that the “prime rate” changes and any changes in the Interest Rate will be effective on 
and after the date of such change and until the next change.  The “prime rate” is set by Bank based 
on various factors, including Bank’s costs and desired return, general economic conditions and 
other factors, and is used as a reference point in pricing some loans.  Bank may price loans to its 
customers at, above, or below its “prime rate.”  Notwithstanding the foregoing, in no event shall 
the Interest Rate at any time be less than zero percent (0.00%).

by mutual agreement between County, acting through its agent, the Navajo County Treasurer, and 
Bank (acting in its sole and absolute discretion), such Scheduled Commitment Expiration Date

operating revenues”, as such term is used in the Act. On the Maturity Date, County shall pay to

connection with the execution and delivery of the Business Loan Agreement 
(Navajo County Districts Revolving Line of Credit), dated July 1, 2025 (the

documents and agreements executed in connection with the Loan 
Agreement and the Note. Pursuant to A.R.S. §§ 11-604.01 et. seq., the 
Board of Supervisors of County may enter into separate and distinct 
revolving lines of credit for each political subdivision of County (hereafter 
referred to as a “District” or “Districts”). The Loan Agreement and the Note 
were approved by a resolution, Resolution Number ___-2025 at a meeting 
of the Board of Supervisors of Navajo County on June 24, 2025 (the 
“Resolution”).  
 
 This opinion is provided to Bank pursuant to Paragraph 3.1.1 of the 
Loan Agreement.  Capitalized terms not otherwise defined herein have the 
respective meanings set forth in the Loan Agreement and the Note. 
 
 We have examined executed copies of the Resolution, the Bank 
Services Agreement, the Loan Agreement, the Note, certificates of officials 
of County and applicable statutes of and relating to the lines of credit made 
available under the Loan Agreement, in each case, as amended to date; 
records of proceedings of the governing body of County during or by which 
resolutions were adopted relating to matters covered by this opinion, and 
certificates of officers of County as to certain factual matters. 
  
 We have made no independent investigation of any of the Districts 
to whom Bank will extend a revolving line of credit under the Loan 
Agreement.  In addition, we have made such other investigations as we have 
deemed necessary to enable us to express the opinions hereinafter set forth.

Loan Documents on behalf of parties thereto other than County and the 
Treasurer, the authenticity of all documents submitted to us as originals and

conformed or photostatic copies.  
 
 Based upon the foregoing, we hereby advise you that in our opinion: 
 
1. County and the Treasurer have the power and authority to execute, deliver and perform the 
Loan Agreement, the Note and the Banking Services Agreement without any action by each 
of the Districts to confirm or ratify such action.

RESOLUTION NUMBER _____-2025
A RESOLUTION OF THE BOARD OF SUPERVISORS OF NAVAJO COUNTY
APPROVING THE FORM AND AUTHORIZING THE EXECUTION AND DELIVERY
OF AN AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE TREASURER OF NAVAJO COUNTY AND
WELLS FARGO BANK, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION PROVIDING FOR SEPARATE
LINES OF CREDIT FOR EACH POLITICAL SUBDIVISION OF THE STATE FOR
WHICH THE COUNTY TREASURER OF NAVAJO COUNTY ACTS AS TREASURER;
RATIFYING ALL ACTIONS TAKEN TO DATE WITH RESPECT TO SUCH
AGREEMENTS.
RECITALS
WHEREAS, Wells Fargo Bank, National Association (the "Bank") entered into a Master
Banking Services Agreement dated June 7, 2023, with Graham County ("Graham County") under
which the Bank agreed to provide certain banking services (such contract being the "Graham
County Contract") and pursuant to the Graham County Contract, other governmental entities that
are members of the Strategic Alliance for Volume Expenditures ("SAVE") purchasing group or that
enter into intergovernmental cooperative purchasing agreements (each an "ICPA") with Graham
County are entitled to procure some or all of the banking services under the Graham County
Contract;
WHEREAS, Navajo County (the "County") is either a member of SAVE or has entered into
an ICPA and therefore is entitled to procure banking services from the Bank; and
WHEREAS, the Bank has agreed to provide certain banking services to the County as
specified in and subject to the terms and provisions of that certain Agreement for Banking Services
dated April 22, 2025, between the County and the Bank (such contract being the "Navajo County
Contract"), for the period commencing July 1, 2025 and ending June 30, 2026, with permitted
extensions pursuant to A.R.S. § 35-325; and
WHEREAS, one of the banking services the Bank is willing to provide pursuant to the
Navajo County Contract is a line of credit for each political subdivision of the state for which the
County Treasurer acts as treasurer pursuant to A.R.S § 11-604.01; and

<!-- page 131 -->
2
WHEREAS, A.R.S. §§ 11-604.01 et. seq., authorizes the Supervisors of the County to enter
into a line of credit agreement on behalf of each individual political subdivision of the state for
which the County Treasurer acts as treasurer; and
WHEREAS, a draft of the Business Loan Agreement (Navajo County Districts Revolving
Line of Credit) providing a line of credit for each qualifying political subdivision of the state for
which the County Treasurer acts as treasurer and to be evidenced by a promissory note has been
provided by the Bank (upon execution and inclusive of the referenced promissory note, the
“Political Subdivisions Agreement”) and has been placed on file with the Clerk of this Board and
presented at the meeting at which this Resolution was adopted; and
WHEREAS, by this Resolution the Supervisors will authorize the execution and delivery
of the Political Subdivisions Agreement, in substantially the form so presented to the Board of
Supervisors, subject to the approval of the Navajo County Attorney.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE BOARD OF SUPERVISORS OF
NAVAJO COUNTY, as follows:
Section 1.  That a draft of the Political Subdivisions Agreement, in substantially the form
on file with the Clerk, is approved and the Chairman of this Board (or any acting Chair of this
Board) and the Treasurer of the County are authorized and directed to execute and deliver the
Political Subdivisions Agreement on file with the Clerk for each qualifying political subdivision
of the state for which the County Treasurer acts as treasurer.
Section 2 . The County Treasurer is named as each political subdivision’s agent for all
purposes of the Political Subdivisions Agreement.  The County Treasurer is authorized to take all
acts and to do all things on behalf of each qualifying political subdivision of the state for which the
County Treasurer acts as treasurer, including, with limitation, requesting amendments to the
Commitment Amount Cap under the Political Subdivisions Agreement, provided that the
Commitment Amount Cap shall not be increased to an amount which exceeds $5,000,000.
Section 3 .  All actions taken by the County Treasurer and any person representing the
County Treasurer with respect to the Political Subdivisions Agreement, and the procedures
pertaining thereto, are hereby ratified and affirmed.  This Resolution shall become effective
immediately upon adoption and execution.

BUSINESS LOAN AGREEMENT 
(NAVAJO COUNTY DISTRICTS REVOLVING LINE OF CREDIT) 
DATE: July 1, 2025 
PARTIES: Borrower: Each of the Districts listed in Schedule I hereto, 
through the Navajo County Treasurer, as their agent, 
which Schedule I may be amended from time to time 
Bank: Wells Fargo Bank, National Association, a national 
banking association, authorized to do business in the 
State of Arizona (“Bank”)
AGREEMENT:  Pursuant to Arizona Revised Statutes Sections 11-604.01 et. seq., (together with 
all amendments and statutes successor thereto, collectively, the “Act”), the Board of Supervisors 
of a county may enter into an agreement with the financial institution authorized to do business in 
the State of Arizona for the purpose of obtaining a line of credit for each of the political 
subdivisions of the county.  The Act further provides that the Navajo County Treasurer is the agent 
for the County and for each political subdivision of the State of Arizona for which the Navajo 
County Treasurer acts as treasurer and may take any action required under an agreement without 
further approval of any governing body of a political subdivision.  The Board of Supervisors of 
Navajo County (the “County”), the Navajo County Treasurer and Bank intend to enter into this 
Agreement and the hereafter-described Note to obtain a line of credit pursuant to the Act for each 
of the districts listed in Schedule I attached hereto (individually a “Borrower” and collectively, 
“Borrowers”), in the respective maximum amounts shown on said Schedule I for each Borrower, 
subject, in each instance, to the then available amount under the Commitment Amount Cap (as 
defined herein), if any, and to evidence all such lines of credit in this Agreement and the Note.  For 
purposes of this Agreement and each line of credit extended to a Borrower evidenced hereunder 
and in the Note, such Borrower shall be acting through the Navajo County Treasurer as its agent 
pursuant to the Act.  For good and valuable consideration, the receipt and sufficiency of which are 
hereby acknowledged, each Borrower and Bank agree as follows:

from time to time.
