limited to white, off-white, beige or tan. The design of other buildings and other structures 
shall, to the extent reasonably feasible and consistent with public safety, use materials, 
colors, textures, screening and landscaping that will  blend the facility into the existing 
environment 
 
11. The applicant shall avoid locating turbines in mountain passes or draws or on cliff edges 
in order to minimize avian and/or bat collisions when wildlife studies show that the 
project would pose a significant risk to avian and/or bat populations. Towers and nacelles 
shall be designed so as not to attract nesting birds or serve as perches for raptors. The 
SUP holder shall refer to the Arizona Game and Fish Department’s and the U.S. Fish and 
Wildlife Services’ wind guidelines that have been developed to aid the project proponents 
in reducing impacts to wildlife. 
 
12. Pre-construction and post-construction wildlife studies shall be developed and performed 
with consideration given to the Arizona Game and Fish Department and U.S. Fish and 
Wildlife Service guidelines. Any wildlife impacts discovered during

Section 1203 – Solar Energy Generation Facilities 
The following provisions shall be specific for the review of Solar Energy Generation Facilities: 
1. Setbacks. All Solar Energy Generation Facilities and structures must comply with setback, 
building height, and performance standards between zones for the zoning district in 
which the system is located, unless the County determines a modified setback is necessary 
to address impacts to existing adjacent uses. 
 
2. A reduction in the setback requirements set forth above in accordance with any or a 
combination of the following circumstances is allowed: 
 
a. The project shares a common property line with another approved Solar Energy 
Generation facility.  
 
b. An irrevocable written consent from an affected property owner has been obtained, 
stating that the owner is aware of the proposed facility and the setback 
requirements imposed by this section, that consent is granted to allow lesser 
setbacks than those specified herein, and that such consent will be memorialized in 
a notice recorded with the Navajo County Recorder to notify future owners of the 
subject property that setbacks are less than those specified herein.  
 
3. Buffering.  Solar Energy Generation Facilities that adjoin residential development shall be 
required to provide adequate screening through the use of fences, walls, landscaping, or 
other structures deemed adequate by Planning and Development Services. 
Section 1204 – Fees 
Fees for Special Use Permits for Renewable Energy Generation Facilities shall be $600.00 plus 
$50.00 per acre, with a fee cap of $25,000.00.

RE: Navajo County Renewable Energy Ordinance
Dear Planning and Zoning Commission Members, 
As president and CEO of the Arizona Technology Council, the states premier trade association representing 750 
science and technology companies, I am writing to respectfully request the Navajo County Planning and Zoning 
Commission approve an ordinance that would promote the construction, siting and operation of utility-
scale renewable energy systems in the county.
As you are likely aware, Navajo County is growing as residents and businesses have relocated and now proudly call 
the county home. As the demand for reliable and affordable energy has increased, a balanced energy portfolio 
emphasizing renewable energy technologies offers the most optimal solutions to meet these needs.
Renewable energy projects have bolstered economic resiliency in rural Arizona. Counties and municipalities that 
have embraced wind and solar projects have experienced the creation of hundreds of local construction jobs and 
permanent technology maintenance jobs. Additionally, these projects have generated millions of dollars in local tax 
revenue, helping fund roads, schools and emergency services  all without tax increases on residents. 
An effective and responsible renewable energy ordinance in Navajo County would forego subjective statutory 
language that hinders the construction of high-quality solar and wind energy projects. Solar facilities and wind farms 
promote continued energy independence and reliability. Expanding renewable energy would keep energy costs 
more stable and affordable while ensuring a more secure energy future for Navajo County residents and 
businesses. 
I respectfully urge you to consider these recommendations when deliberating on this critical ordinance.

On behalf of BluEarth Renewables, I would like to sincerely thank you for hosting the recent Renewable

the County is taking to consider community input while seeking to balance economic development with 
environmental stewardship. 
At BluEarth, we are committed to being a responsible partner to Navajo County and all local stakeholders. 
We support the County’s goals of ensuring the thoughtful siting of renewable energy projects and are eager 
to continue working collaboratively as this ordinance is refined.  
A key area of interest for us has been the proposed setbacks that have been raised in the Listening Sessions. 
We recognize the concerns that have been raised and, while we aim to maintain flexibility to responsibly 
site projects, we are willing to support a 0.5 mile setback from national forest lands. This is more than 3.5 
times the current setback requirement of 1.1 times the total turbine height (assuming a turbine of 650 feet  
or less). Furthermore, this mirrors the proposed setback for legal dwelling units and reflects a significant 
commitment on our part. Based on our internal research, this would be one of the most restrictive non-
residential setbacks for wind projects in the country  and shows a clear indication of our BluEarth’s 
willingness to work with the County and stakeholders to  prioritize harmony with public lands and 
community values.  
We also want to emphasize our commitment to responsible decommissioning.  The industry has recognized 
the concerns that stakeholders have raised regarding the recycling of materials at end of project life and 
significant efforts are underway to advance the reuse of and recyclability of major project components (e.g. 
turbine blades and tower materials).  At the end of the project’s life, we pledge to recycle turbines  and 
components using the best available technology at that time. As advancements are made in materials and 
processes, we will remain committed to using methods that minimize environmental impact and promote 
a circular economy.

choose.

What is AriSEIA?
• The Arizona Solar Energy Industries Association (AriSEIA) is the 
solar, storage, and electrification trade association for the 
State of Arizona.
• We advocated for pro-renewables policy at every level of 
government.
• We are especially active at the Arizona Corporation 
Commission (ACC) and Arizona legislature.
• We also have a robust consumer protection body of work.
• We are an Arizona nonprofit.
• We engage with local governments on renewables ordinances.

<!-- page 938 -->
Why is there so much more development?
• The Arizona utilities engage in long term resource planning 
every three years.
• Those plans reflect that they each need to double or triple 
their entire fleets in the next 10-15 years.
• This is due to very significant load growth from the increase in 
data centers, manufacturing, electrification, electric vehicles, 
extreme weather, and population growth.
• Therefore, to meet reliability, the utilities must build more 
generating resources.

<!-- page 939 -->
Why build renewables?
• All new resources must compete in utility all source requests 
for proposals (ASRFPs).
• An ASRFP allows different projects to compete on several
factors, including price, location, and development timeline.
• Solar and wind are cost competitive resources.
• Renewables use less water than traditional resources.
• Renewables do not have volatile fuel expenses.
• Renewables can be built quickly.
• Renewables do not contribute to air pollution compliance 
problems under the Clean Air Act (CAA).

<!-- page 940 -->
Why build renewables here?
• The location of renewables projects has to do with several
factors:
• The projects need to be on relatively flat ground.
• The land must be available either for sale or lease.
• The land must be located near transmission lines or other 
infrastructure like substations.
• The resource (wind or solar) needs to be good in that region.
• The land cannot be a national park, state park, mountainous region, 
body of water, etc.
• The land must comply with local zoning laws. 
• Projects must have geographic diversity to maintain grid reliability.

<!-- page 941 -->
What is in it for the local community?
• Hundreds of jobs during construction for every project.
• ~$500,000 annually in personal property taxes per project.
• ~$22 million in taxes over the life of each project.
• ~$350 million in economic development over the life of each 
project.
• Significant water savings over other land uses.
• Increased grid reliability by having projects closer and more 
geographically dispersed from each other.
• Lower cost electricity because renewables are a low-cost resource 
and projects that are not owned by the utility don’t have an added 
profit margin.

<!-- page 942 -->
What about the bad stories I’ve heard about 
renewables?
• There is a lot of misinformation about renewables.
• We created a myth busting website, because we ran into it so 
often.
• Solar is not more expensive.
• Solar does not use more water.
• Solar panels are not toxic and will not pollute your water.
• Solar panels are not solely produced in China and are not unique from 
other appliances in this regard.
• Solar panels do not cause a heat island.
• Batteries are not uniquely unsafe.
• Renewables are not overfilling landfills.

<!-- page 943 -->
Where can I find more information?
• Many local governments are considering ordinances related to 
renewables.
• There are many resources available to help:
• We have a website with myth busting resources and several economic and 
water reports.
• Interstate Renewable Energy Council (IREC) has a SolSmart program that 
provides technical assistant on solar permitting.
• American Clean Power Association has model ordinances.
• Solar Energy Industries Association has an Arizona solar census.
• The American Planning Association has a zoning practice guide for battery 
storage.
• National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) 855 has the standard for the 
installation of stationary energy storage systems.
• AriSEIA is available for any questions and can help with redlines or other 
technical expertise.

Summary of Impacts 
There is a common misconception that wind energy projects do not contribute to the economy 
nor generate tax revenues for local governments.  However, wind projects across all counties in 
Arizona are subject to personal property taxes on equipment and, thus, generate significant 
revenue for local taxing jurisdictions as outlined in this report.  In addition, wind projects can 
generate use taxes levied on non -exempt equipment for the State (but these additional State 
taxes are not included in this analysis).   
 
This report estimates the impacts of a typical wind energy  project producing up to 240 MW of 
power to be located in Coconino County.  While a wind project of this size could be up to 20,000 
acres, the actual footprint of disturbed land would cover an estimated 175 acres and allow 
existing grazing to continue .  A wind project of this size is generally in range with recent power 
purchase contracts announced by Arizona Public Service and Salt River Project, two of the state’s 
largest electric utilities. 
 
The taxable original cost of a project of this size is estimated at $ 320.0 million.  The  taxable 
original cost is subject to personal property tax using a 25 -year straight-line depreciation with a 
10% floor.  The full cash value of renewable energy equipment is 20% of the depreciated cost of 
the equipment per ARS 42 -14155.  This full cash value is subject to Arizona personal property 
taxes over the life of the project (assumed to be construction plus 39 years in this analysis). 
 
Impact Summary 
During construction, an estimated $698,900 in tax revenues and 268 jobs would be created in 
the local economy from this example project.  In addition, over the life of the project, more than 
$9.5 million in tax revenue would be generated by personal property tax on equipment.  These 
taxes would directly benefit the county, its special districts (such as county fire, flood and library 
districts), and local school districts.  Furthermore, employees working on the project generate an 
estimated $2.3 million in tax revenues.   
 
In total, this example Coconino County Wind Project would generate an estimated $12.4 million 
in tax revenues during the life of the project.  The total economic output of the project over the 
life of the project is estimated at $862.5 million.

Economic Impact Methodology 
 
Economic impact analysis examines the economic implications of an activity in terms of output, 
earnings, and employment.  For this study, the analysis focused on the construction impacts as 
well as the ongoing operations including direct expenditures by the residents. 
 
The different types of economic impacts are known as direct, indirect, and induced, according to 
the manner in which the impacts are generated.  For instance, direct employment consists of 
permanent jobs held by project employees.  Indirect employment is t hose jobs created by 
businesses that provide goods and services essential to the operation or construction of the 
project.  These businesses range from manufacturers (who make goods) to wholesalers (who 
deliver goods) to janitorial firms (who clean the buildings).  Finally, the spending of the wages 
and salaries of direct and indirect employees on items such as food, housing, transportation and 
medical services creates induced employment in all sectors of the economy, throughout the 
region. These secondary effects are captured in the analysis conducted in this study. 
 
Multipliers have been developed to estimate the indirect and induced impacts of various direct 
economic activities.  IMPLAN developed the m ultipliers used in this study and were selected 
based on the land use type.  The multipliers  used for this project  represent the construction of  
power and communication as well as electric power generation for ongoing operations.   
 
The construction multipliers specific to Coconino County are used in this study.  For the Wind energy 
generation multiplier, an average of similar economies was used, as the current multiplier set for 
Coconino County does not exist.   
 
The economic impact is categorized into three types of impacts: 
 
(1) Employment Impact – the total wage and salary and self -employed jobs in a 
region.  Jobs include both part time and full-time workers. 
 
(2) Earnings Impact – the personal income, earnings or wages, of the direct, indirect 
and induced employees.  Earnings include total wage and salary payments as well 
as benefits of health and life insurance, retirement payments and any other non -
cash compensation. 
 
(3) Economic Output – also referred to economic activity, relates to the gross receipts 
for goods or services generated by the company’s operations.

<!-- page 954 -->
Coconino County Wind energy Project Impact 
Elliott D. Pollack & Company   
www.arizonaeconomy.com 8 
Economic impacts are by their nature regional in character.  Such impacts are best illustrated 
when not assigned to a specific municipality  or locality, although clearly the primary impact of 
job creation would be in the municipality and county where the project is located.  Indeed,  many 
communities in the surrounding region would also benefit from the operations of the project. 
 
Fiscal Impact Methodology 
 
Fiscal impact analysis studies the public revenues associated with a particular economic activity.  
The primary revenue sources of local, county, and state governments (i.e., taxes) are analyzed to 
determine how an activity may affect the various jurisdict ions.  This section would evaluate the 
impact of the project on State, county and local school districts.  
 
The fiscal impact figures cited in this report have been generated from information provided by 
a variety of sources including the U.S. Bureau of the Census; the U.S. Department of Labor; the 
Internal Revenue Service; the State of Arizona; the Arizona Tax Research Association; and the 
U.S. Consumer Expenditure Survey.  Elliott D. Pollack &  Company has relied upon the estimates 
of operating revenues outlined in this study.   
Fiscal impacts are categorized by type in this study, similar to economic impact analysis.  The 
major sources of revenue generation for governmental entities are calculated based on ongoing 
operations. Employees would spend part of their salaries on local goods and services and pay 
taxes on the homes they occupy.  This spending would contribute to revenues collected by the 
State that are ultimately shared with local governments.   
The project would be exempt from prime contracting transaction privilege tax (under ARS 42 -
5075(b)(7) and ARS 42- 5061).  However, there is still substantial value from equipment that 
would increase the personal property revenues for the County.  Revenues would also be 
generated from secondary sources of employee generated revenue.  The following is a 
description of the applicable revenue sources that would be considered for this analysis.   
 
Primary Taxes Generated by Project 
• Personal Property Tax 
Renewable energy projects are centrally assessed by the Arizona Department of Revenue.  
The total original cost is used to calculate the full cash value.  The depreciation schedule is 
then based on straight-line depreciation over the useful life (currently 25 years capped at 
90% of taxable original cost per ARS 42 -14155).  The full cash value factor for renewable 
energy is 20% and the assessment ratio of 15% is applied for a total taxable value each year. 
 
Secondary Taxes Generated by Employees

<!-- page 955 -->
Coconino County Wind energy Project Impact 
Elliott D. Pollack & Company   
www.arizonaeconomy.com 9 
The following tax rates are applied to the spending of direct, indirect and induced employees.   
 
• Transaction Privilege Tax 
The State, counties, and local cities in Arizona charge sales tax on retail goods  and utility 
usage.   The sales tax rate for the State is 5 .6%.  Portions of this tax are redistributed 
through revenue sharing to counties and cities throughout Arizona based on population.  
The weighted average tax rate for local governments is 2.41 %.  Based on data from the 
U.S. Consumer Expenditure Survey, the projected extent of retail spending and resulting 
sales tax receipts was calculated.  
• Property Tax 
Given that the location of the example project is unknown, the value of the land was not 
estimated and, thus, r eal property taxes for the land are not calculated in this report.  
However, the employees would be subject t o residential property tax in Arizona with an 
assessment ratio of 10%.   In order to estimate property taxes, the assessed full cash value 
of the occupied space along with the projected value of a typical housing unit has been 
calculated.   
 
• State Shared Revenues 
Each municipality in Arizona receives a portion of State revenues from four different 
sources - State sales tax (see description above), State income tax, vehicle license tax 
and highway user tax.  The formulas for allocating these revenues are primarily based 
on populatio n.  Counties also share in the revenue sources of the State, with the 
exception of income tax.   
State Income Tax 
The State of Arizona collects taxes on personal income.  The tax rate used in the 
analysis averages about 1.6% for earnings.  These percentages are based on the 
most recently available income tax data from the State and the projected wage 
levels of jobs created by the construction and operations impact.  This tax is applied 
to the wages and earnings of direct and indirect employment.  Portions of this tax 
are redistributed through revenue sharing to cities throughout Arizona based on 
population. 
HURF Taxes 
The State of Arizona collects specific taxes for the Highway User Revenue Fund 
(HURF).  Both the registration fees and the motor vehicle fuel tax (gas tax) are 
considered in this analysis.  The motor vehicle fuel tax is $0.18 per gallon and is 
calculated based on a vehicle traveling the Arizona statewide average of 12,000 
miles per year at 16.6 miles per gallon.  Registration fees average $65 per employee

<!-- page 956 -->
Coconino County Wind energy Project Impact 
Elliott D. Pollack & Company   
www.arizonaeconomy.com 10 
in the State of Arizona.  These factors are applied to the projected direct and 
indirect employee count.  Portions of these taxes are distributed to cities and 
counties throughout Arizona based on a formula that includes population and the 
origin of gasoline sales. 
Vehicle License Tax 
The vehicle license tax is a personal property tax placed on vehicles at the time of 
annual registration.  This factor is applied to the projected direct, indirect and 
induced employee count.  The average tax used in this analysis is $343 and portions 
of the total collections are distributed to the Highway User Revenue Fund.  The 
remaining funds are shared between cities and counties in accordance with 
population-based formulas. 
The above tax categories represent the largest sources of revenues that would be generated to 
the various jurisdictions .  The revenue impacts do not include certain revenue sources such as 
corporate income taxes.  All tax collections represented in this analysis are gross collections and do 
not take into consideration any incentives or development agreements that may occur.

Summary of Impacts 
There is a common misconception that solar projects do not contribute to the economy nor 
generate tax revenues for local governments.  However, solar projects across all counties in 
Arizona are subject to personal property taxes on equipment and, thus, generate significant 
revenue for local taxing jurisdictions as outlined in this report.  In addition, solar projects can 
contribute to increased real property taxes as well as generate use taxes levied on non -exempt 
equipment for the State (but these additional State taxes are not included in this analysis).   
 
This report estimates the impacts of a typical solar project to be located in Navajo  County.  This 
example solar power generating facility would sit on an estimated 1,200 acres and produce up to 
200 MW of power and includes the addition of 200 MW (4 hours) of battery storage.  A facility of 
this size is generally in range with recent power purchase contracts announced by Arizona Public 
Service and Salt River Project, two of the state’s largest electric utilities. 
 
The taxable original cost of a  project of this size is estimated at $528.0 million.  The taxable 
original cost is subject to personal property tax using a 30 -year straight-line depreciation with a 
10% floor for solar and 15 -year straight-line depreciation with a 10% floor for battery storage.  
The full cash value of renewable energy equipment is 20% of the depreciated cost of the 
equipment per ARS 42-14155.  This full cash value is subject to Arizona personal property taxes 
over the life of the project (40 years for the solar facility and 20 years for battery storage). 
 
Impact Summary 
During construction, an estimated $682,100 in tax revenues and 285 jobs would be created in 
the local economy from this example project.  In addition, over the life of the project, more than 
$17.1 million in tax revenue would be generated by personal property tax on equipment.  These 
taxes would directly benefit the county, its special districts (such as county fire, flood and library 
districts), and local school districts.  Furthermore, employees working on the project generate an 
estimated $840,000 in tax revenues.   
 
In total, this example Navajo County Solar Project would generate an estimated $ 18.7 million in 
tax revenues during the life of the project.  The total economic output of the project over the life 
of the project is estimated at $193.5 million.

Economic Impact Methodology 
 
Economic impact analysis examines the economic implications of an activity in terms of output, 
earnings, and employment.  For this study, the analysis focused on the construction impacts as 
well as the ongoing operations including direct expenditures by the residents. 
 
The different types of economic impacts are known as direct, indirect, and induced, according to 
the manner in which the impacts are generated.  For instance, direct employment consists of 
permanent jobs held by project employees.  Indirect employment is t hose jobs created by 
businesses that provide goods and services essential to the operation or construction of the 
project.  These businesses range from manufacturers (who make goods) to wholesalers (who 
deliver goods) to janitorial firms (who clean the buildings).  Finally, the spending of the wages 
and salaries of direct and indirect employees on items such as food, housing, transportation and 
medical services creates induced employment in all sectors of the economy, throughout the 
region. These secondary effects are captured in the analysis conducted in this study. 
 
Multipliers have been developed to estimate the indirect and induced impacts of various direct 
economic activities.  IMPLAN developed the m ultipliers used in this study and were selected 
based on the land use type.  The multipliers  used for this project  represent the construction of  
power and communication as well as electric power generation for ongoing operations.   
 
The construction multipliers specific to Navajo  County are used in this study .  For the solar 
generation multiplier, an average of similar economies was used, as the current multiplier set for 
Navajo County does not exist.   
 
The economic impact is categorized into three types of impacts: 
 
(1) Employment Impact – the total wage and salary and self -employed jobs in a 
region.  Jobs include both part time and full-time workers. 
 
(2) Earnings Impact – the personal income, earnings or wages, of the direct, indirect 
and induced employees.  Earnings include total wage and salary payments as well 
as benefits of health and life insurance, retirement payments and any other non -
cash compensation. 
 
(3) Economic Output – also referred to economic activity, relates to the gross receipts 
for goods or services generated by the company’s operations.

<!-- page 967 -->
Navajo County Solar Project Impact 
Elliott D. Pollack & Company   
www.arizonaeconomy.com 8 
Economic impacts are by their nature regional in character.  Such impacts are best illustrated 
when not assigned to a specific municipality  or locality, although clearly the primary impact of 
job creation would be in the municipality and county where the project is located.  Indeed,  many 
communities in the surrounding region would also benefit from the operations of the project. 
 
Fiscal Impact Methodology 
 
Fiscal impact analysis studies the public revenues associated with a particular economic activity.  
The primary revenue sources of local, county, and state governments (i.e., taxes) are analyzed to 
determine how an activity may affect the various jurisdict ions.  This section would evaluate the 
impact of the project on State, county and local school districts.  
 
The fiscal impact figures cited in this report have been generated from information provided by 
a variety of sources including the U.S. Bureau of the Census; the U.S. Department of Labor; the 
Internal Revenue Service; the State of Arizona; the Arizona Tax Research Association; and the 
U.S. Consumer Expenditure Survey.  Elliott D. Pollack &  Company has relied upon the estimates 
of operating revenues outlined in this study.   
Fiscal impacts are categorized by type in this study, similar to economic impact analysis.  The 
major sources of revenue generation for governmental entities are calculated based on ongoing 
operations. Employees would spend part of their salaries on local goods and services and pay 
taxes on the homes they occupy.  This spending would contribute to revenues collected by the 
State that are ultimately shared with local governments.   
The project would be exempt from prime contracting transaction privilege tax (under ARS 42 -
5075(b)(7) and ARS 42-5061).  However, there is still substantial value from solar equipment that 
would increase the personal property revenues for the County.  Revenues would also be 
generated from secondary sources of employee generated revenue.  The following is a 
description of the applicable revenue sources that would be considered for this analysis.   
 
Primary Taxes Generated by Project 
• Personal Property Tax 
Renewable energy projects are centrally assessed by the Arizona Department of Revenue.  
The total original cost is used to calculate the full cash value.  The depreciation schedule is 
then based on straight-line depreciation over the useful life (currently 30 years capped at 
90% of taxable original cost per ARS 42 -14155).  The full cash value factor for renewable 
energy is 20% and the assessment ratio of 15% is applied for a total taxable value each year.

<!-- page 968 -->
Navajo County Solar Project Impact 
Elliott D. Pollack & Company   
www.arizonaeconomy.com 9 
Secondary Taxes Generated by Employees 
The following tax rates are applied to the spending of direct, indirect and induced employees.   
 
• Transaction Privilege Tax 
The State, counties, and local cities in Arizona charge sales tax on retail goods  and utility 
usage.   The sales tax rate for the State is 5 .6%.  Portions of this tax are redistributed 
through revenue sharing to counties and cities throughout Arizona based on population.  
The weighted average tax rate for local governments is 2.7%.  Based on data from the U.S. 
Consumer Expenditure Survey, the projected extent of retail spending and resulting sales 
tax receipts was calculated.  
• Property Tax 
Given that the location of the example project is unknown, the value of the land was not 
estimated and, thus, r eal property taxes for the land are not calculated in this report.  
However, the employees would be subject t o residential property tax in Arizona with an 
assessment ratio of 10%.   In order to estimate property taxes, the assessed full cash value 
of the occupied space along with the projected value of a typical housing unit has been 
calculated.   
 
• State Shared Revenues 
Each municipality in Arizona receives a portion of State revenues from four different 
sources - State sales tax (see description above), State income tax, vehicle license tax 
and highway user tax.  The formulas for allocating these revenues are primarily based 
on populatio n.  Counties also share in the revenue sources of the State, with the 
exception of income tax.   
State Income Tax 
The State of Arizona collects taxes on personal income.  The tax rate used in the 
analysis averages about 1.6% for earnings.  These percentages are based on the 
most recently available income tax data from the State and the projected wage 
levels of jobs created by the construction and operations impact.  This tax is applied 
to the wages and earnings of direct and indirect employment.  Portions of this tax 
are redistributed through revenue sharing to cities throughout Arizona based on 
population. 
HURF Taxes 
The State of Arizona collects specific taxes for the Highway User Revenue Fund 
(HURF).  Both the registration fees and the motor vehicle fuel tax (gas tax) are 
considered in this analysis.  The motor vehicle fuel tax is $0.18 per gallon and is 
calculated based on a vehicle traveling the Arizona statewide average of 12,000

<!-- page 969 -->
Navajo County Solar Project Impact 
Elliott D. Pollack & Company   
www.arizonaeconomy.com 10 
miles per year at 16.6 miles per gallon.  Registration fees average $65 per employee 
in the State of Arizona.  These factors are applied to the projected direct and 
indirect employee count.  Portions of these taxes are distributed to cities and 
counties throughout Arizona based on a formula that includes population and the 
origin of gasoline sales. 
Vehicle License Tax 
The vehicle license tax is a personal property tax placed on vehicles at the time of 
annual registration.  This factor is applied to the projected direct, indirect and 
induced employee count.  The average tax used in this analysis is $343 and portions 
of the total collections are distributed to the Highway User Revenue Fund.  The 
remaining funds are shared between cities and counties in accordance with 
population-based formulas. 
The above tax categories represent the largest sources of revenues that would be generated to 
the various jurisdictions .  The revenue impacts do not include certain revenue sources such as 
corporate income taxes.  All tax collections represented in this analysis are gross collections and do 
not take into consideration any incentives or development agreements that may occur.

Executive Summary 
This report provides an analysis of water consumption of various land uses in Arizona, 
offering insight into how land use decisions impact water resource commitments in the arid 
Southwest. Understanding these differences is crucial for decision making in a reas facing 
water scarcity and where efficient resource allocation is essential. The objectives of this 
analysis were to develop proxy water use estimates for land use types that might be 
considered alternative to the development of solar projects in Arizo na, to highlight the 
differences in the water demands of each land use type and by power generation facility type, 
and to clarify the disparities in water demand to enable decision-makers to promote efficient 
water use and sustainable land development across the region. 
In particular, t his report summarizes the water demands of various land use categories in 
Arizona in comparison to the relatively low water demands of solar projects. Alternative land 
uses including irrigated agriculture, subdivision development, industrial, and commercial  
are found to consistently require larger volumes of water than solar. From a water 
conservation perspective, solar is a preferred land use in the arid Southwest because of its 
modest water footprint. To demonstrate the benefits of solar, this analysis qu antifies the 
water demands of alternative land uses based on data from Arizona Department of Water 
Resources (ADWR or “the Department”) and other publicly available sources.  
The results of the analysis clearly demonstrate that water use by solar facilities is 
significantly lower than that of potential alternative land uses in Arizona. Average water use 
across all sectors analyzed in this effort is 3.4 acre-feet1 per acre ( AF/acre), which is 100 
times the use of solar ( 0.03 AF/acre). In particular, data centers were found to use 6.3 
AF/acre on average, which is 200 times the amount used by solar. Metro Phoenix is the 
second-largest data center market in the nation in large part because of the availability of 
power and land2. In conclusion, compared to other land use categories evaluated, water use 
by solar is negligible. When compared to water requirements of natural gas  and nuclear  
power generation facilities , these power sources require 25-100 times the water 
requirements of solar facilities to produce one megawatt (MW) (4.3 AF/MW for natural gas 
and 18.7 AF/MW for nuclear compared to 0.16 AF/MW for solar).

Summary of Findings 
Water use in Arizona is categorized under three main sectors: municipal, industrial, and 
agricultural. According to ADWR, 74% 3  of the state’s total annual water use is irrigated 
agriculture followed by municipal use at 20% 4. Industrial water use accounts for only 6% of 
the state’s total water use. Industrial use of land across Arizona is also minimal relative to 
other uses. In Maricopa and Pinal counties, industrial uses account for only 0.47% of total 
land use5. Solar generation projects are a type of industrial use that require a minimal volume 
of water 6. Such low water requirements may be a reason there is no ADWR conservation 
program for solar facilities, programs that seek to regulate water use for a variety of facilities 
and water use types7. This analysis provides context on solar water use as compared to other 
water uses in Arizona.  
WestWater compiled sector-level water use data reported to ADWR and from other sources 
within the state’s Active Management Areas (AMAs) to develop and analyze proxy water 
demand estimates of annual average water use by relevant alternative land uses. Alternative 
land uses include agriculture, residential (subdivisions), manufacturing, data centers, and 
industrial uses. Industrial uses include large turf facilities, primarily golf courses, dairy 
operations, cattle feedlot operations, and power generation facilities.  
Estimated water use for each sector by acre and MW (as applicable) is summarized in Table 
1. The highest estimated water use across all AMAs during the 2019 -2023 analysis period 
was attributed to data centers  at 6.3 AF/acre, followed by turf and agricultural irrigation at 
4.1 AF/acre, and manufacturing at 3.6 AF/acre. Natural gas and nuclear power facilities, for 
which water use data were reported to ADWR,  require 4.3 AF/MW and 18.7 AF/MW, 
respectively. Solar facility water use is extremely low in terms of both a per acre and per MW

Conclusions 
The results of this analysis clearly demonstrate that water use by solar facilities is 
significantly lower than that of  potential alternative land uses. In fact, solar water use is 
virtually zero, which cannot be said of any other alternative land use. Other land uses utilized 
water at significantly higher rates than solar facilities. Average water use across the sectors 
analyzed for this effort is 3.4 AF/acre, which is 100 times the use of solar facilities  (0.03 
AF/acre). In particular, data centers were found to use 6.3 AF/acre on average, which is 200 
times the amount used by solar. Nuclear power was found to use 18.7 AF/MW, which is 100 
times the amount used by solar  (0.16 AF/MW). As compared to the other water use 
estimates, solar facility water use is negligible.

Appendix A: Data and Methodology  
This analysis primarily utilizes AMA annual 
report data from ADWR. AMAs encompass 
the most populated areas of the state 
and account for approximately 80% of 
statewide water use 8. Within the AMAs, 
water use exceeding a certain volume is 
highly regulated and therefore water 
may only be utilized pursuant to a water 
right. For these reasons, AMAs are the 
only areas of the state for which 
comprehensive, up -to-date water use 
data are available. In addition, the 
management plans detail several 
mandatory conservation programs for 
various water use types. Water users 
within AMAs are required to annually 
report the water use, and facilities that 
fall into a required conservation program 
must report supplement al use 
information.  
ADWR data include total use by irrigation rights and various industrial subsectors including 
golf courses, feedlots, dairy, and power. Supplemental data were also provided including, as 
applicable, associated irrigation acres, acres of landscaped area, number of animals, 
volume of product produced, and amount of power generated.  Although ADWR data are only 
available for the AMAs, as it is the most robust water use dataset within Arizona, these values 
are used as a proxy for other water use in the same sectors in Arizona.  
In addition, data from the Central Arizona Groundwater Replenishment District (CAGRD) and 
Census Bureau (CB) were used to develop water use estimates for subdivisions 9 . This 
included 2018-2022 CAGRD data on the number of new CAGRD member land lots and their 
projected water demand. Lot size data from the CB Survey of Construction in 2021 were also 
used10. In addition to these sources, this analysis also utilized the ADWR Supply and Demand

Assessments methods appendix 11  to develop water use sector demand estimates. 
Governmental reports and other publicly available information were referenced to develop 
manufacturing and data center water demands. 
WestWater developed estimates of annual water use for the following sectors and 
subsectors: Irrigation,  Golf Course , Feedlots, Dairy, Subdivisions, Manufacturing, Data 
Center, and Power. Solar water use can be captured in two ways: 1) volume by acre and 2) 
volume per amount of power produced. To develop water use estimates that are comparable 
to solar use, WestWater used two common units. For water use that is associated with the 
size of the land, water estimates are developed per acre. For the power sector , water use is 
not directly related to the size of the land where the facility is sited. Instead, the volume of 
water is expressed as AF/MW.  
Irrigation 
To develop estimates for irrigation water, ADWR annual report data were filtered to irrigation 
rights or rights that fall under the base or best management plans’ conservation programs. 
Once the data were filtered, the total reported annual use in AF was d ivided by the number 
of acres associated with each right. Although some annual reports include irrigated acres, it 
is not required by the Department. As a result, this estimate does not necessarily represent 
water use per irrigated acre, although it may be representative of agricultural land. 
Irrigation water use varies by AMA as summarized in Figure 3. The Phoenix AMA had the 
highest water use, averaging 5.1 AF/acre over the 5 years of reported data.  The Santa Cruz 
and Prescott AMAs had the lowest use, with an average of 2.3 AF/acre and 2.4 AF/acre 
respectively. Overall, the average irrigation use across all years and AMAs was 4.1 AF/acre.

Golf Course 
The industrial water use sector consists of various turf subsectors including golf. Turf related 
facilities are required to report up-to-date data on the number of turfed, low water use, and 
water surface acres present. These acres were summed to determine total acreage for golf. 
The total reported annual water use was then divided by the total number of acres for golf for 
an AF/acre estimate by facility. 
Water use by golf courses is typically related to the amount of high intensity water use (turf 
and water features) and the efficiency of irrigation infrastructure. The 5-year average water 
use for golf courses ranges from 3.2 AF/acre to 4.2 AF/acre across the AMAs.  Overall, golf 
course water use average s 4.1 AF/acre. Golf water use is lower on courses in the Prescott 
AMA, where precipitation tends to be higher. Water use by turf for golf courses is summarized 
in Figure 4.

Feedlots/Dairy  
ADWR annual reports for feedlots include data on the number of animals at each facility by 
month. These data were summed to develop an annual number of animals per facility. The 
total reported water use was then divided by the number of animals at each facility for an 
AF/animal estimate. Feedlot designs include one acre of land per 100 heads of cattle, which 
includes space for pens, alleys and feed roads 12 . To determine a per -acre estimate for 
feedlots, the volume of AF per animal was multiplied by the number of animals per acre.  
ADWR data for feedlots were reported in the Phoenix and Pinal AMAs.  
Feedlots use slightly more water in the Pinal AMA and average 1.5 AF/Acre, as compared to 
1.1 AF/acre in the Phoenix AMA, as summarized in Figure 5. Across all facilities and all years, 
the average feedlot use is 1.4 AF/acre.

Dairy use was estimated based on  ADWR’s Supply and Demand Assessments (SDA) 
methods. The ADWR SDA estimates a range of water use per type of cow, including water use 
for consumption, dust suppression, and other facility uses. The estimates range from 0.02 to 
0.04 AF/animal/year, with lower water use representing calves and the highest water use 
reflecting use b y lactating cows. The average water use among all animal types was 0.03 
AF/animal/year. Dairy facilities require one acre per 75 heads of cattle 13. Using the ADWR 
SDA method and assuming 75 animals per acre results in an estimated water use of 2.2 
AF/acre. 
Subdivisions 
CAGRD Annual Operations Reports from 2018 -2022 were used as the basis for developing 
subdivision water use estimates. These reports include estimates of projected annual

widely and was not used to develop a per acre estimate. Average lot size is also variable, 
however, data from the CAGRD and CB were used to estimate average lot sizes in Arizona. 
CAGRD estimates average lot sizes of approximately 9,000 square feet (sq ft) and 12,000 sq 
ft in the Phoenix and Tucson areas respectively14. The CB conducts a Survey of Construction,

Manufacturing Facilities 
Arizona is becoming a hub for manufacturing, in large part due to significant federal and state 
investment and favorable economic and geographic conditions. There are little to no annual 
water use report data on manufacturing facilities in publicly available datasets, such as 
those maintained by ADWR  and relied upon in this analysis . Taiwan Semiconductor 
Manufacturing Company (TSMC) and Intel are two major companies with facilities in Arizona 
who have publicly provided estimates of their facility  water usage.  TSMC estimates using 
4.75 million gallons per day (MGD) or 5,321 AF annually at its 1,100-acre facility, equivalent 
to 4.8 AF/acre. Intel estimates using 1.5 MGD or 1,680  AF annually at its 700 -acre facility, 
equivalent to 2.4 AF/acre16. Together these facilities use an estimated 3.6 AF/acre annually 
on average. 
Data Centers 
As data center facilities are relatively new in Arizona, ADWR does not collect annual reports 
from these water users. However, data can be collected from company sustainability 
reports, local water management plans, press releases, and news articles. Water use 
information for 30 facilities was collected by WestWater from across the United States. Of

of the facility and the amount of power used at the facility. To develop a comparable water

Water use was correlated with total size at the facility as shown in Figure 6. Water use by size

Power  
ADWR annual report data were used to estimate water use for the power subsector 
consisting of nuclear and natural gas. While there are other power generation facility types 
in Arizona outside the AMAs, this analysis only considers those AMA facilities whose water 
use is reported to ADWR.  ADWR data also included information on power generated at each 
facility by month. However, these data were inconsistently reported and the units used were 
often unclear. To ensure a comparable unit, ADWR use d publicly avai lable information on 
each of the facilities to determine the MW capacity.17  The total water use was divided by the 
generating capacity of each facility to estimate an AF/MW.  
ADWR collects annual report data for eight power facilities  in the AMAs , including one 
nuclear and seven natural gas facilities. Water use was filtered to the type of facility as the 
difference in reported use across facility type was vast. Over the five -year analysis period,

Solar 
Because solar facilities use such a small amount of water, ADWR does not require annual 
water usage reporting and therefore data are limited. In general, ADWR-exempt uses 
account for less than 100 AF of water per year18.  
The National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) completed a study on water supply and 
demand conditions impacting the solar industry, which includes estimates of solar water 
use19. The study includes water consumption estimates for photovoltaic (PV) solar. PV is a 
non-thermal renewable energy technology that does not require water but can use a 
relatively small amount of water primarily for washing panels.  This technology is commonly 
used in solar facilities because it is a renewable, non -polluting, and inexhaustible energy 
source. The estimated median water use rate for solar is 25 gallons per megawatt hours 
(MWh) or 0.0001 AF/MWh, which represents the volume of water per unit of electricity 
generation. NREL demonstrates that solar uses water at a rate of virtually zero to produce 
electricity.

Most solar projects in the Southwest US are never washed during operation, however for this 
analysis, the NREL water use per MWh estimate was utilized to evaluate an example 200 MW 
solar project on 1,200 acres. A facility of this size is generally in the range with recent power 
purchase contracts announced by Arizona Public Service and Salt River Project, two of 
Arizona’s largest electric utilities . According to FreeingEnergy, one MW of solar power 
produces 2,146 MWh of solar energy 20. In this example, the total water use of the facility 
would be equivalent to 32.9 AF. Over a 200 MW, 1,200-acre facility, this equates to an annual 
water use estimated to total 0.16 AF/MW and 0.03 AF/acre.

The

could
 
benefit
 
from
 
the
 
jobs,

and
 
grid
 
stability
 
that
 
local,
 
renewable
 
energy
 
can
 
provide.
  Utility-scale  solar  projects,  for  example,  create  local  construction  jobs  and  permanent  
maintenance
 
and
 
operation
 
jobs.
 
They
 
also
 
generate
 
tax
 
revenue
 
that
 
supports
 
and
 
funds
 schools,  emergency  services,  and  infrastructure,  all  without  burdening  taxpayers.  The  Box  Canyon  Solar  Park in  Pinal  County,  for  instance,  is  projected  to  generate  $43  million  in  local  tax  benefits,  300  temporary  and  4  permanent  jobs,  and  add  $134.6  million  in  economic  activity.  In  
Navajo
 
County,
 
similar
 
benefits
 
could
 
help
 
fund
 
more
 
public
 
services,
 
provide
 
jobs,
 
and
 
lower
 
taxes
 
for
 
residents.
 
  Navajo  County  could  also  benefit  from  utility-scale  renewable  energy  projects  because  the  
power
 
they
 
produce
 
is
 
more
 
reliable
 
and
 
affordable
 
than
 
power
 
from
 
traditional
 
generation.
 Having  stable  power  during  Arizona’s  scorching  summers  is  a  matter  of  life  and  death.  When  paired  with  battery  storage,  renewable  power  generation  is  now  just  as  reliable as  power  produced  from  traditional  fossil  fuels.  The  cost  of  producing  renewable  energy  has  dropped  significantly  over  the  last  decade  and  this  trend  is  expected  to  continue.  Having  more  local  utility-scale  renewable  energy  projects  can  help  create  a  more  stable  power  grid  and  lower  
electricity
 
costs
 
for
 
Navajo
 
County
 
residents
 
and
 
businesses.
  As  Arizonans,  we  appreciate  that  renewable  energy  generation  is  far  less  taxing  on  water  
resources,
 
compared
 
to
 
traditional
 
forms
 
of
 
energy
 
generation.
 
This
 
is
 
especially
 
important
 
in

<!-- page 987 -->
Navajo  County,  which  contains  multiple  tribal  lands,  including  the  Navajo  Nation.  The  Navajo  Nation  and  tribal  lands  in  general  have  a  well-documented  struggle with  getting  adequate  water  supplies and  infrastructure for  their  needs.  When  water  is  scarce,  any  conservation  effort  is  an  important  one.  Traditional  gas  and  coal  generation  plants  typically  consume between  2,000  and  3,000  liters  of  water  per  generated  MWh.  Solar  generation  plants  only  consume  446  liters  per  
MWh.
 
Wind
 
power
 
plants
 
consume
 
even
 
less
 
water
 
at
 
279
 
liters
 
per
 
MWh.
 
This
 
significant
 
improvement
 
in
 
water
 
usage
 
per
 
MWh
 
generated
 
makes
 
renewable
 
energy
 
generation
 
much
 
more
 
advantageous
 
for
 
Navajo
 
County.
  We  know  that  siting  for  any  infrastructure  projects  should  be  done  meticulously  and  thoughtfully  
with
 
a
 
clear

of
 
all

and
 
impacts.
 
Not
 
every
 
location
 
is
 
suited
 
equally,
 
and
 
local
 
preferences
 
and
 
needs
 
should
 
be
 
prioritized.
 
It

also
 
important
 
to
 
note
 
that
 
keeping
 
the
 
doors
 
open
 
to
 
the
 
benefits
 
that
 
this
 
infrastructure
 
can
 
provide
 
would
 
be
 
a
 
service
 
to
 
Navajo
 
County's
 
future.

  Table  4.  General  Components  of  a  Community  Benefits  Negotiation  Component  Description  
Initiation  Who  initiates  negotiations?  ●  Developer-initiated:  Developer  seeks  community  input  ●  Community-initiated:  Community  seeks  out  potential  developers,  e.g.,  through  an  RFP  (e.g.,  Babbitt  Ranch  &  Henvey  Inlet)  
Leadership  Who  represents  the  community?  ●  Agency-led  ●  Community-led  
Enlisting  help  Who  is  needed  to  help  the  community  with  negotiations?  ●  “Staff,  facilitators,  or  others  with  technical  expertise  such  as  lawyers…that  help  forward  local  priorities”  
Discussions  &  Negotiations  
●  Extensive  discussions  between  representatives  of  impacted  communities  and  wind  developers  ●  Exploring  local  impacts  and  opportunities  for  investment  in  the  community,  which   ●  May  leverage  existing  comprehensive  plans  for  community  priorities

Appendix  B:  Community  Benefits  Databases  
World  Resources  Institute  (WRI)  Community  Benefits  Database  
 
The
 
WRI
 
Community
 
Benefits
 
Database
 
catalogs
 
publicly
 
available
 
community
 
benefit
 
commitments
 
tied
 
to
 
clean
 
energy
 
projects
 
across
 
the
 
U.S.
 
It
 
includes
 
categories
 
like
 
workforce
 
development,
 
local
 
hiring,
 
and
 
environmental
 
justice.
 
●  Strengths:  ○  Offers  broad  coverage  of  benefit  types  and  projects  across  multiple  technologies.  ○  Highlights  trends  and  best  practices  in  community  benefit  design.  ○  Emphasizes  transparency  and  equity  in  project  development.  ●  Weaknesses:  ○  Limited  to  publicly  disclosed  commitments;  may  not  reflect  what  is  ultimately  
delivered.
 ○  Lacks  detailed  geographic  filters  or  searchable  project  outcomes.  ○  Doesn’t  consistently  include  enforceability  or  monitoring  mechanisms.  ●  Guidance  for  Use:  
 
Use
 
the
 
WRI
 
database
 
as
 
a
 
benchmarking
 
tool
 
to
 
understand
 
the
 
range
 
of
 
benefits
 
other
 
communities
 
have
 
secured
 
from
 
similar
 
projects.
 
It’s
 
especially
 
useful
 
in
 
early-stage
 
negotiations
 
to
 
shape
 
requests
 
for
 
proposals
 
(RFPs)
 
or
 
community
 
benefit
 
agreements
 
(CBAs)
.
 
 
National  Renewable  Energy  Laboratory  (NREL)  Community  Benefits  
Database
 
 
NREL’s
 
Community
 
Benefits
 
Database
 
tracks
 
how
 
renewable
 
energy
 
projects
 
incorporate
 
economic
 
and
 
social
 
benefits
 
into
 
their
 
design,
 
including
 
specific
 
agreements
 
or
 
commitments
 
made
 
to
 
host
 
communities.
 
●  Strengths:  ○  Provides  detailed  examples  of  benefit  categories  (e.g.,  education,  job  creation,  
infrastructure).
 ○  Highlights  replicable  models  and  strategies  for  inclusive  development.  ○  Developed  by  a  trusted  federal  lab  with  deep  energy  sector  expertise.  ●  Weaknesses:  ○  Coverage  is  selective  and  still  evolving;  not  comprehensive.  ○  May  not  include  informal  or  undocumented  community  commitments.  ○  Does  not  evaluate  effectiveness  or  outcomes  of  the  benefits  promised.  ●  Guidance  for  Use:

the

database
 
to

precedents

benefit

- In December 2022, Apex Clean Energyâ€™s Conservation Grant Program
awarded a $200,000 conservation grant on behalf of the El Sauz and Young wind
projects. The grant went to Bat Conservation International, which will work with
Texas Parks and Wildlife and the Texas Department of Criminal Justice to restore
or relocate a colony of nearly one million Mexican free-tailed bats from a critical
historic bat roost in an old cotton warehouse in Huntsville, Texas. Additionally,
the grant will support bat education, outreach, and research at the site.  Through
Apex Clean Energyâ€™s Conservation Grant Program, each renewable energy
project commercialized by Apex contributes a sum of money, proportional to the
size of the project, to support local or regional wildlife conservation, reforestation

- Green Mountain Power established a Good Neighbor Fund of approximately
$180,000 annually (for the first ten years of the wind project's operation) to
provide benefits to the towns that are within five miles of the wind project but
don't receive tax revenues like the host town (Lowell) does. Total annual payment
is determined based on power generation at the wind project, and each town's
portion is determined by how much of the town's area is in the wind project's five-
mile radius. In 2016, Eden received $77,420, Albany received $69,885,
Craftsbury received $33,851, and Westfield and Irasburg each received $10,000.
The towns determine how to use these funds, including for investments in
infrastructure and facilities; for example, Craftsbury residents voted to use the
funds to invest in a solar energy system to help cover municipal electric needs.

Property devaluation due to Wind & Solar Farms Data 
Dear _______________________________________________, 
               
The impact of wind and solar farms on property values in rural areas has been a topic of significant concern. 
Recent studies and real estate data have shed some light some on this issue, revealing that the presence of 
these costly eye soars of so called renewable energy installations can and do indeed have a negative effect on 
nearby property values as well as real property that is within eye site. 
 
Wind and solar farms, while championed for their over inflated and often misrepresented environmental 
benefits, disrupt the natural beauty that draws people to rural areas—think rolling hills, open fields, or 
forested vistas, think of the beauty of the White Mountains, replaced or interrupted by towering twirling 
turbines, blinking lights or sprawling light glaring, heat generating solar panels. 
Studies and simple anecdotal evidence suggest that proximity to these installations can lower property values, 
primarily due to diminished visual appeal, noise (in the case of wind turbines), and total loss of tranquility. Not 
to mention the killing off of birds, that includes Bald & Golden Eagles, bats and insects, greatly disrupting the 
natural order of things. 
For example, research on wind farms has shown mixed results, but some studies, like one from the Journal of 
Real Estate Research (2016), found that properties within a few miles of turbines can see value drops of 5-
15%, depending on factors like distance, density of turbines, and the original appeal of the area. Solar farms, 
though quieter, can still transform large swathes of land into what some describe as an "industrial eyesore," 
potentially deterring buyers who prioritize scenic views. 
The mechanism here is straightforward: rural properties often trade on their seclusion, natural beauty, and 
recreational potential. When industrialization encroaches—especially in areas marketed as pristine—demand 
will soften. Buyers seeking a peaceful retreat will look elsewhere, shrinking the pool of potential purchasers 
and pushing prices down. This effect is more pronounced in regions where tourism or second-home markets 
(e.g., vacation cottages) bolster property values, as visual degradation directly undercuts those industries. 
Farmers hosting turbines or panels might see a steady income, providing the Wind or Solar Corporation make 
money off the units, and if they don’t go bankrupt and abandon the site. These leases only benefit the land 
owner, and there are no guarantees on most of these leases. This greatly hurts and disturbs all the other 
property owners in the surrounding areas, for miles around on many different levels.

<!-- page 1131 -->
2 
 
Resentment is a huge factor that these communities’s face, and you BoS, should be acutely aware of it, as a 
lot of this resentment is directed at you for making these Special Use Permits available to these Corporations 
that don’t care about what is important to our community. The community is devastated at these future 
catastrophic changes in our landscapes, our wild life, our way of life. This is another huge factor in depressing 
the real estate market and our economy.  
Tourism-dependent spots like the White Mountains are devalued more and take longer to sell because of the 
impact of being with in eye site, of what once was a pristine landscape, that has been turn into an 
industrialized eye soar, that has become permanently  “Spoiled”.   
Data Wind Farms 
Research indicates that wind turbines lead to a decrease in property values, particularly for homes in closer 
proximity to these installations. The extent of this impact varies depending on factors such as distance, 
visibility, and the size of the wind farm: 
Properties within 1 mile of wind turbines have experienced average value decreases of 7%, with houses in 
rural areas seeing drops of up to 23% [1] 
Some studies have found that homes within 1.2 miles of wind turbines can see value reductions ranging 
from 25% to 40% [1][2] 
The effect of wind turbines on property values can extend up to 5 to 10 miles from the installation 
site[1]And extend all the way to “Within Eye Site”. Example is the eye sores now seen from Show Low on 
260 looking towards Snow Flake. The complete ruin of the aesthetic charm of the expansive landscape. 
Data Solar Farms 
In rural areas, solar farms DO devalue nearby real property. However, The data found on the impact Solar 
Farms have on real property values have mostly been done by the building Solar Corporations or a hired by 
them, and not by independent studies and therefore are deemed biases and unreliable. 
So simply based on Location, Location, Location: as the main moto in selling real property: 
Lets visit some realities that are directly in front of our faces: 
Rural settings are more sensitive to devaluing due to their reliance on landscape and agricultural identity. 
 
Rural property values often hinge on open space, scenic views, and agricultural use. A solar farm swaps fields 
or forests for panels and fencing, which can feel like an industrial intrusion. Think of a 100-acre cornfield 
turning into a sea of metal and glass—buyers seeking that pastoral vibe will look elsewhere.  
 
Issues like inverter hum or panel glare can stand out in quiet, low-density areas, greatly diminishing any 
tranquility, again people will look elsewhere.

<!-- page 1132 -->
3 
 
Most all rural communities see solar farms as a threat to their economic backbone—farming & ranching—
leading to a resentment and community oppression. 
 
The devaluing effect is way more pronounced when solar farms replace agricultural land or natural 
landscapes, as this will alter the rural character that resident’s value, by introducing an industrial element like 
panels, fencing, or inverters.  
 
Visual changes—replacing open fields with rows of panels—can reduce aesthetic appeal, a key feature in rural 
property markets.  
 
Noise from equipment like inverters or concerns about glare might also play a role. 
 
The loss of productive farm & ranching land can spark local resistance, amplifying perceptions of reduced 
desirability. 
 
Additionally, the property owners know that these giant Solar Farms are killing birds and incest’s by the 
hundreds of thousands which again, completely disrupts the natural way of thing in a farm land.  
Residences might decide to move away from the White Mountains in search of a more tranquil pristine area in 
which to live. 
Cumulative Impact 
The combined effect of these so called renewable energy projects on rural communities can be substantial: 
When aggregated across all affected properties, the total loss in value due to wind farms in some areas has 
been estimated at billions of dollars [1][6] 
For solar installations, the cumulative loss in property values has been calculated to reach $1.7 billion in 
some regions. 
Factors Influencing Value Loss 
Several factors contribute to the depreciation of property values near wind and solar farms: 
Visual impact on the landscape 
Potential noise pollution from wind turbines 
Loss of rural character and open space 
Concerns about health effects from low-frequency sound (wind turbines) 
Reduced marketability of affected properties

<!-- page 1133 -->
4 
 
Long-term Considerations 
While some studies suggest that the impact on property values may diminish over time, the long-term effects 
remain a concern for many homeowners and communities. The industrialization of rural landscapes through 
these large-scale energy projects continues to be a contentious issue. These Farms permeably destroy any 
preservation of rural property and it’s values along with the way of every day life. 
If there are more of these Wind and Solar Farms built here in the White Mountains, property will get devalued 
even more as time goes on, simply because people will go elsewhere for generations to come in search of 
tranquility, open spaces, beautiful night skys, and undisturbed wild life. 
And now that the real truth is being revealed, with more information coming out daily on the entire 
“Renewable” boondoggle hoax,  on just how inefficient, expensive and environmentally devastating both 
these Industrialized Wind and Solar Farms are, people are going to grow less and less tolerant of them. 
In conclusion, the evidence strongly suggests that Wind and Solar farms DO have a significant negative impact 
on property values in rural areas.  
For generations, this mountain will suffer because of these Wind and Solar Farms, and we are only on the 
subject of residences suffering from devalued real property. 
Let me remind all of you, especially you 3 Native American BoS, your land is scared to you, and rightly so. We 
are all in this together and OUR White Mountains, and all Gods Creations that are in it, is sacred to all of us! 
We the people of Navajo County, strongly speak that we are commanded by God, to be good stewards of the 
land we are given, to nurture and protect it. Wind and Solar is not following that command, on any level.  
As our representatives’, you BoS, must consider the vital economic and social consequences your decisions 
you make on these Wind and Solar Farms.  
On behalf people of Navajo County and throughout the White Mountains, we ask you to answer this 
question for generations to come:  
Are you going to be the people that save our White Mountains from catastrophic devastation and choose to 
save it, and keep it pristine, and hold it sacred as the people you serve do, for generations to come? 
Or are you going to choose to destroy it? 
We will know you by your decisions, and we will remember you for it.  
Sincerely,

The devaluing effect is way more pronounced when solar farms replace agricultural land or natural 
landscapes, as this will alter the rural character that resident’s value, by introducing an industrial element like 
panels, fencing, or inverters.  
 
Visual changes—replacing open fields with rows of panels—can reduce aesthetic appeal, a key feature in rural 
property markets.  
 
Noise from equipment like inverters or concerns about glare might also play a role. 
 
The loss of productive farm & ranching land can spark local resistance, amplifying perceptions of reduced 
desirability. 
 
Additionally, the property owners know that these giant Solar Farms are killing birds and incest’s by the 
hundreds of thousands which again, completely disrupts the natural way of thing in a farm land.  
Residences might decide to move away from the White Mountains in search of a more tranquil pristine area in 
which to live. 
Cumulative Impact 
The combined effect of these so called renewable energy projects on rural communities can be substantial: 
When aggregated across all affected properties, the total loss in value due to wind farms in some areas has 
been estimated at billions of dollars [1][6] 
For solar installations, the cumulative loss in property values has been calculated to reach $1.7 billion in 
some regions. 
Factors Influencing Value Loss 
Several factors contribute to the depreciation of property values near wind and solar farms: 
Visual impact on the landscape 
Potential noise pollution from wind turbines 
Loss of rural character and open space 
Concerns about health effects from low-frequency sound (wind turbines) 
Reduced marketability of affected properties

Dear Navajo County Board of Supervisors, Economic Development & Planning and Development,  
              
The impact of wind and solar farms on property values in rural areas has been a topic of significant concern. 
Recent studies and real estate data have shed some light some on this issue, revealing that the presence of 
these costly eye soars of so called renewable energy installations can and do indeed have a negative effect on 
nearby property values as well as real property that is within eye site.
Wind and solar farms, while championed for their over inflated and often misrepresented environmental 
benefits, disrupt the natural beauty that draws people to rural areasthink rolling hills, open fields, or 
forested vistas, think of the beauty of the White Mountains, replaced or interrupted by towering twirling 
turbines, blinking lights or sprawling light glaring, heat generating solar panels.
Studies and simple anecdotal evidence suggest that proximity to these installations can lower property values, 
primarily due to diminished visual appeal, noise (in the case of wind turbines), and total loss of tranquility. Not 
to mention the killing off of birds, that includes Bald & Golden Eagles, bats and insects, greatly disrupting the 
natural order of things.
For example, research on wind farms has shown mixed results, but some studies, like one from the Journal of 
Real Estate Research (2016), found that properties within a few miles of turbines can see value drops of 5-
15%, depending on factors like distance, density of turbines, and the original appeal of the area. Solar farms, 
though quieter, can still transform large swathes of land into what some describe as an "industrial eyesore," 
potentially deterring buyers who prioritize scenic views.
The mechanism here is straightforward: rural properties often trade on their seclusion, natural beauty, and 
recreational potential. When industrialization encroachesespecially in areas marketed as pristinedemand 
will soften. Buyers seeking a peaceful retreat will look elsewhere, shrinking the pool of potential purchasers 
and pushing prices down. This effect is more pronounced in regions where tourism or second-home markets 
(e.g., vacation cottages) bolster property values, as visual degradation directly undercuts those industries.
Farmers hosting turbines or panels might see a steady income, providing the Wind or Solar Corporation make 
money off the units, and if they dont go bankrupt and abandon the site. These leases only benefit the land 
owner, and there are no guarantees on most of these leases. This greatly hurts and disturbs all the other 
property owners in the surrounding areas, for miles around on many different levels.
