RESEARCH INTO CONCERNS SUBMITTED 
REGARDING OTHER RENEWABLE PROJECTS 
 
The following inquiries regarding other renewable projects were raised: 
 
A. Pink Cliffs: 
 
During the Heber listening session, it was asked if a follow-up had been conducted on  
the 2008 Pink Cliffs wind farm. No evidence was found of a "Pink Cliffs" wind farm from 2008. 
However, AES is constructing the West Camp Wind Farm near the Pink Cliffs geological 
feature in Navajo County, though not within the area itself. This project adheres to the current 
renewable energy ordinance. 
 
Alternatively, "Pink Cliffs" may refer to NovoPower's Pink Cliffs Land Company near 
Snowﬂake, which includes landﬁlls, water storage facilities, and ash disposal from Novo 
BioPower. Novo RePower is exploring options for a nearby coal plant, such as converting it to 
natural gas or repurposing steam for industrial use. 
 
B. Underestimated Decommissioning Costs: 
 
It was  asserted that the Birch Solar Project in Ohio underestimated potential 
decommissioning costs that would be shifted to the local government. According to the 
LimaOhio.com news source, the Birch Solar P roject was denied by the Ohio Power Siting 
Board. Birch Solar ﬁled to dismiss its appeal of the denial in January 2025. Before revoking 
its appeal, Birch Solar argued that the board was over -reliant on public sentiment and did 
not conduct its own analysis of the project's potential beneﬁts. For background, signiﬁcant 
pushback from the community  relating to this project was rece ived, and the Power Siting 
Board denied the application due to “a lack of public interest, convenience, and necessity  
as required by Ohio law. ”  
 
It was also asserted that decommissioning costs were underestimated for the Palmer’s 
Creek wind project in Minnesota. This assertion is accurate, with the original 
decommissioning bond amount being $400,000 compared to the estimated actual 
decommissioning cost of  $7.39 million , or about $410,000 for each of the 18 turbines. 
Palmer’s Creek wind farm became operational in 2019 and continues to operate to this day. 
According to the West Central Tribune, Chippewa County had placed a moratoriu m on 
renewable energy projects , which has since been lifted after the county updated its 
ordinance to increase setbacks, li mit development on prime farmland, and mandate up -
front funding to cover future decommissioning costs. The updated ordinance reﬂects 
lessons learned from existing projects like Palmer’s Creek.

<!-- page 1161 -->
C. Dismantling of 15-Year-Old German Wind Farm: 
 
Concern was voiced over a 15-year-old wind farm in Germany that was dismantled due 
to economic challenges. This comment appears to reference the Alpha Ventus offshore test 
ﬁeld with a 20 -year life expectancy. Renewable Energy Hamburg noted in 2020 that, in 
Germany, the impetus to explore the dismantling of offshore wind turbines comes mainly 
from wind farm operators, as they are responsible for decommissioning. The current 
regulations are ambiguous and do not specify precisely whether the foundations need to be 
removed completely or partially. Some confusion also remains as to how the turbine blades 
should be recycled. Nonetheless, the study also indicates that the imminent dismantling of 
the ﬁrst offshore wind farms in the North Sea region has the potential to be come a new 
growth market with opportunities for companies, municipalities, and port operators.  
 
In November 2024, German offshore wind and hydrogen developers joined forces to 
build an offshore electrolyzer demonstrator at Alpha Ventus. This proposed project aims to 
demonstrate the feasibility and efficiency of producing green hydrogen directly at sea using 
offshore wind power and electrolyzers.  
 
D. Abandoned Wind Farms: 
 
A claim was made that Italy’s Monday RC Wind Farm  was abandoned months after 
operation, leaving decades of cleanup to local authorities. In an article for Science Direct, it 
was identiﬁed that this wind power plant, also known as the Butera wind power plant, was 
abandoned due to incomplete construction of the necessary substations stemming from 
municipal mismanagement of funds. No formal decommissioning has occurred. 
 
Another example provided by stakeholders is Monte Arci wind farm in Italy. This wind farm 
was built in 2000 and abandoned after a few months of operation because the turbines were 
technologically obsolete. Both Butera and Monte Arci were among the subjects of scientiﬁc 
research published in Energy Sustainable Development in 2025. Researchers concluded 
that the common causes for sustainable energy project abandonment in Europe and South 
America are poor planning, economic and technological issues, and lack of management. 
There are regulatory gaps that exist in count ries like Italy, Spain, Venezuela, and Argentina, 
which complicate decommissioning abandoned wind farms. The study's authors advocate 
for stronger regulations, including mandatory decommissioning plans, and emphasize the 
importance of recycling and restoring renewable energy landscapes to ensure sustainability.  
 
E. Federal Aviation Administration: 
 
Some aviation concerns were raised by stakeholders. The Town of Springerville, located 
in Apache County, sent a letter to the FAA regarding concerns about the Lava Run Wind Farm, 
and the Eagar Town Council opposed the project.  Navajo County's current wind ordinance 
mandates FAA compliance, and Planning & Development Services conﬁrmed that the FAA 
issues determinations of no hazard before wind energy projects come to the county for

<!-- page 1162 -->
approval. Navajo County also sends renewable energy projects to Luke Air Force Base for 
review to ensure there is no interference with military training paths. 
 
F. Global Reclamation: 
 
A claim that  only 12% of global renewable energy sites have been properly reclaimed 
could not be substantiated. It is estimated that 11,000 wind turbines have been 
decommissioned in the United States since 1992, which represents a signiﬁcant portion of 
the more than 86,000 turbines built from 1981 – 2024. According to the Environmental and 
Energy Study Institute (EESI), over 190,000 contaminated sites (mine lands, brownﬁeld sites, 
Superfunds, and landﬁlls) can be remediated and re -purposed for renewable energy 
generation. Further, the Office of Energy Eff iciency & Renewable Energy indicates that over 
14 GW of U.S. renewable energy projects have already been fully or partially repowered, with 
analysts expecting an additional 16 GW of full or partial repowers through 2026.  
 
The Office of Energy Efficiency & Renewable Energy identiﬁes that decommissioning a 
wind energy project, including turbine removal and site restoration, can take 6 –24 months, 
depending on project size. Some infrastructure, like power lines and substations , may be 
reused during repowering, while access roads on private land may be retained at the 
landowner’s discretion. Land lease agreements and local ordinances typically require 
restoring sites to pre -project conditions, which may involve de -compacting soil, reseeding 
vegetation, and replacing drainage tiles. While most above -ground infrastructure is 
removed, some below-ground components may remain to minimize environmental impacts 
such as soil disturbance, erosion, and water pathway disruptions. The agreed-upon removal 
depth must balance environmental concerns with future land use needs, including 
agriculture. 
 
G. Unpaid Taxes: 
 
A claim was made that  some Oklahoma counties have spent $17 million ﬁghting wind 
companies over unpaid taxes. The claim appears to reference the Rock Falls Wind Farm in 
Oklahoma. According to the Oklahoman newspaper, company executives initially claimed 
that Rock Falls Wind Farm  was tax -exempt and ﬁled lawsuits to nullify property tax 
assessments. However, Rock Falls abandoned its tax-exempt claim and paid more than $2.2 
million in property taxes in 2018.  
 
H. Failed Decommissioning Bonds: 
 
It was  mentioned that bond companies have failed to pay decommissioning bonds, 
leaving domestic and international communities in costly legal battles. The ﬁrst case study 
cited was the Viking Energy Wind Farm in Scotland. Construction  began on this project  in 
2019 without the required bond in place. However, the bond was established in 2022, and 
Viking Energy Wind Farm  is currently operational. Another example cited was  the Murra 
Warra Wind Farm in Australia, where community concern arose because the project risked

<!-- page 1163 -->
ﬁnancial collapse. However, the project was acquired by Partners Group in 2020 and 
remains operational.  These case studies do not represent bond company failures.  
 
In the United States, the Ipswich Wind Independence LLC turbine was damaged by an 
electrical ﬁre in 2018. The project lacked a decommissioning bond, and the Town of Ipswich 
in Massachusetts is delaying the decommissioning process while it decides the best course 
of action. Possible solutions include instating a  bond, escrow funding, or a 
decommissioning fund managed by the town. Like the international examples, the Ipswich 
project is not a failure by a bond company but rather a lack of bonding.  
 
I. Oklahoma Setback Policies: 
 
Policies related to setbacks in Oklahoma were highlighted. The proposed House Bill 2751 
would apply to counties that meet certain wind speed (<9.5 mph) and population density 
(>8.5 per square mile) requirements. This bill propose s setbacks of 1.5x the tip height of a 
wind turbine from the property line or a half mile from an occupied dwelling, whichever is 
greater. Other energy-related measures include bills that would allow businesses producing 
electricity only for themselves to a void regulation as a public utility; limiting wind turbines 
near military installations and operations; placing setbacks on solar energy and industr ial 
battery storage facilities; establishing an advisory committee to study renewable energy 
solutions and how the agriculture industry might beneﬁt; and requiring electric utilities 
seeking to build new facilities to solicit and acquire a Certiﬁcate of Authority from the 
Corporation Commission. 
 
J. Property Values: 
 
Several residents were concerned about property values decreasing due to wind farm 
proximity. There have been several peer -reviewed, U.S.-focused research studies on this 
topic that have found that, while wind turbines generally do not have any widespread, long-
term impact on property values, the construction of a wind farm close (~1 mile) to 
residences in more populated areas can have a short-term impact on property values.  
 
Research in 2013 from the Berkel ey National Laboratory found that if property value 
impacts from wind turbines existed, they were too small and/or too infrequent  to result in 
any widespread, statistically observable impact. Follow-up studies from 2015 and 2016 
were published in the Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics and the Journal of Real 
Estate Research, which found similar results. In 2023, Berk eley Lab published its most 
comprehensive study with data spanning 34 states, 428 unique wind projects, and nearl y 
half a million transactions within 5 miles of projects . The authors found that property value 
effects were evident beginning after the project was announced and continuing through the 
construction period, but abated 3 -5 years after operations began. These effects were 
concentrated in counties with higher population densities (>250,000) and were not evident 
in rural areas.

<!-- page 1164 -->
K. Nantucket Turbine Failure: 
 
One stakeholder raised concerns over a wind turbine blade failure in Nantucket. This 
concern relates to an offshore wind turbine. In July 2024, a catastrophic failure of a wind 
turbine blade at the Vineyard Wind offshore project, located approximately 15 miles south 
of Nantucket, resulted in widespread environmental and public health concerns. The 351 -
foot blade, manufactured by GE Vernova, fractured due to a manufacturing defect involving 
"insufficient bonding, " a ﬂaw that should have been detected by quality assurance protocols. 
Debris from the broken blade, including sharp ﬁberglass fragments, washed up along 
Nantucket's southern beaches, leading to beach closures and raising alarms about potential 
impacts on marine life and local industries. The incident prompted federal authorities to 
suspend operations at the entire wind farm pending a thorough investigation.   
 
L. Harm to Wildlife: 
 
Stakeholder concerns about the impact of wind turbines on wildlife are supported by 
scientiﬁc research and national assessments. According to the American Wind Wildlife 
Institute (2021), land-based wind energy can pose risks to birds and bats through collisions 
with turbine blades and habitat disruption, particularly affecting raptors and migratory tree 
bats, which may experience population -level impacts. Similarly, a 2021 study in Biological 
Conservation found that wind facilities can lead to increased mortality, behavioral changes, 
and habitat avoidance among birds and mammals, with effects varying by species and 
proximity to turbines.  
 
The United State s Geological Survey employs aeroecology scientists to study how the 
aerial habitat of ﬂying animals intersects with the growth of wind energy development. The 
USGS scientists have studied wildlife -wind energy interactions for decades to determine 
which species are commonly impacted and to identify ways to reduce impacts from wind 
energy production. Because of this research, scientists have developed decision -making 
tools that help to plan the location for new wind facilities in places where the risk to wildlife 
is lower. One study showed that systems put in place to automatically slow and temporarily 
shut off wind turbine blades when golden eagles are nearby  are effective at reducing eagle 
fatalities.  
 
The United States Fish & Wildlife Service notes that studies have indicated that relatively 
low raptor fatality rates are found at most modern wind energy developments and that there 
are lower turbine-related bat deaths  at facilities in the west. According to FWS, important 
factors to consider when assessing potential risks include the level of bird use and behavior 
at the site. Will Cresswell, professor of biology at the University of St . Andrews in Scotland, 
suggests that the impacts of renewable energy on land animals can be mitigated by placing 
turbines on agricultural land because it is already compromised in terms of biodiversity and 
already experiences high disturbance. In this way, both energy and food can be produced 
from the same loss of natural habitat, more or less.

integrating more renewable energy sources such as wind and solar onto our grid, Arizona can 
ensure a reliable and cost -effective supply of power while other sources of energy come 
online. Thank you for your time and consideration. 
 
JOSEPH CITY: Ashley thanked Navajo County for hosting discussions and emphasized her 
commitment to collaborating with the county and stakeholders on a renewable energy 
project. As an Arizona native, Bunch shared that the project aims to provide signiﬁcant 
beneﬁts to  the county, including tax revenue and both part -time and full -time job 
opportunities. BluEarth Renewables is dedicated to the area, not only as developers but also 
as operators, ensuring long -term involvement and stewardship in the community. The 
company seeks to maintain strong relationships with local stakeholders, address resident 
concerns, and contribute positively to the region's social and economic growth. They aim to 
support local utilities and participate in transforming the energy sector to meet the 
increasing demand for reliable renewable energy in Arizona. 
 
LETTER: On behalf of BluEarth Renewables, I would like to sincerely thank you for hosting the 
recent Renewable Energy Ordinance Listening Sessions and providing an opportunity for all 
stakeholders to offer feedback on the proposed updates to Navajo County’s renewa ble 
energy ordinance. We value the thoughtful approach the County is taking to consider 
community input while seeking to balance economic development with environmental 
stewardship. At BluEarth, we are committed to being a responsible partner to Navajo County 
and all local stakeholders. We support the County’s goals of ensuring the thoughtful siting 
of renewable energy projects and are eager to continue working collaboratively as this 
ordinance is reﬁned. A key area of interest for us has been the proposed setbacks that have 
been raised in the Listening Sessions. We recognize the concerns that have been raised and, 
while we aim to maintain ﬂexibility to responsibly site projects, we are willing to support a 
0.5 mile setback from national forest lands. This is more than 3.5 times the current setback 
requirement of 1.1 times the total turbine height (assuming a turbine of 650 feet or less). 
Furthermore, this mirrors the proposed setback for legal dwelling units and reﬂects a 
signiﬁcant commitment on our part. Based on our internal research, this would be one of the 
most restrictive non-residential setbacks for wind projects in the country and shows a clear 
indication of our BluEarth’s willingness to work with the County and stakeholders to prioritize 
harmony with public lands and community values. We also want to emphasize our

<!-- page 1168 -->
4 
 
commitment to responsible decommissioning. The industry has recognized the concerns 
that stakeholders have raised regarding the recycling of materials at end of project life and 
signiﬁcant efforts are underway to advance the reuse of and recyclability of major project 
components (e.g. turbine blades and tower materials). At the end of the project’s life, we 
pledge to recycle turbines and components using the best available technology at that time. 
As advancements are made in materials and processes, we will remain committed to using 
methods that minimize environmental impact and promote a circular economy. 
Furthermore, we believe in the importance of protecting private property rights. Our 
landowner partners are generational stewards of the land, and it’s critical they maintain the 
ability to use their property in ways that support their families and livelihoods —including 
participating in clean energy development if they so choose. Lastly, BluEarth is deeply 
invested in the communities where we operate. Beyond the signiﬁcant local tax revenues our 
projects generate, we are proud to commit to a $50,000 annual community fund in Navajo 
County to support local initiatives and organizations. We also provide annual scholarship 
opportunities to local students in ou r project areas to help support the next generation of 
leaders. We thank you again for the opportunity to share our feedback and look forward to 
continued collaboration to create a policy that beneﬁts the County, its residents, and 
Arizona’s energy future.

NAME: Matthew Pagan 
CITY: Andover, MA

COMMENT: 
Honorable Members of the Navajo County Board of Supervisors, Enel North America 
appreciates the opportunity to provide public testimony on renewable energy development 
within these listening sessions. Enel is a leading developer, owner, and operator of ove r 80 
renewable energy plants. Enel has been active in Arizona and Navajo County for the past

projects is a win-win for counties and the residents that live there. As utilities seek additional 
energy to meet growing demand for businesses and households, solar will continue to play 
a vital role in maintaining a reliable and cost-effective power source for Arizona. Beyond just 
meeting growing energy demand, we’re excited to bring signiﬁcant economic beneﬁts to this 
part of the state by developing domestic energy, made here in America. This includes new 
jobs, economic investments, land lease payment to local landowners, and new tax revenue 
for improvements to roads, schools, and other public services for Navajo County residents.  
We would suggest maintaining the ordinance as that is a good, workable model for 
development and the community. Enel would suggest the following as key shared interests 
as the County explores the potential for new renewable energy development: 1. Community 
Beneﬁts. Ensure that there is enough information available to the County to provide

to the community, including responsible decommissioning processes. 2. Streamlined 
Regulatory Process & Efficient Permitting Timelines. For the County, the public, project 
landowners, and project developers it’s important to have timelines that are clear, efficient, 
and avoid regulations that unnecessarily delay and draw out the government permit decision 
making process. Having certainty around timelines for the process provides transparency 
and help everyone work toward meeting those timelines, including the time for public input. 
3. Private Property Rights. The vast majority of our projects are on private property, with land 
lease agreements and payments between Enel and local landowners. Landowners deserve 
the freedom to put their ground into productive use as they see ﬁt. Whether for crops, cattle,

<!-- page 1170 -->
6 
 
or a cell tower, we trust that private property owners know what’s best for their land and their 
families. We suggest avoiding regulations that take away landowners' independence and 
dictate what landowners can and cannot do with their property. This inclu des avoiding 
setback levels too great or other regulations that impede on property rights. Regulations like 
this could also prevent landowners from diversifying revenue streams that help sustain 
multigenerational future land uses. Thank you for your time a nd consideration.  We look 
forward to our work together on future energy projects that beneﬁt Navajo County residents 
and help meet the growing energy demands for all of Arizona. Sincerely, Matthew Pagan, 
Development Manager II, Business Development, West  Region, Enel Green Power North 
America.

NAME: Travis Brown 
CITY: Vancouver, WA 
PLATFORM: Online Survey 
COMMENT: 
SB Energy appreciates the opportunity to provide input on Navajo County’s efforts to develop 
a solar ordinance. SB Energy operates nearly three (3) gigawatts of solar projects, with an 
additional 1.3 gigawatts under construction across the United States. Solar projects 
contribute signiﬁcant local tax payments to the local school district, public health services 
district, the local college, ﬁre district assistance fund, and several other Navajo County 
organizations. Solar projects have many other community beneﬁts, including: •Solar 
projects provide family-wage paying job opportunities during construction, operations, and 
decommissioning stages; • Solar provides reliable energy to the local utility- energy grid to 
serve customers in the state; •Solar has low to zero emissions and little to no water usage 
during project operations; • Solar h as low visual impacts due to the limited height of the 
panels and associated equipment •Notably, solar energy has continued support at the 
national level and President Trump’s Energy Secretary Chris Wright stated in March 2025 the 
Administration supports a nything that adds to “affordable, reliable, secure energy” and 
indicated the Administration supports the rapidly growing role of solar and are in favor of 
moving forward on battery storage projects. Solar and wind energy ordinances should not be 
developed under one renewable energy ordinance. There are signiﬁcant differences 
between wind energy and solar that require distinct approaches to develop, construct, 
operate, and decommission solar projects. SB Energy respectfully requests that Navajo 
County draft  separate solar and wind ordinances to recognize these differences. Key 
differences include the following: • Viewshed Impacts: o Solar viewshed impacts are low. 
Solar panels are typically lower than 12 feet in height and do not obstruct view shed. Due to 
their low viewshed impacts setbacks requirements from residences or municipalities for 
solar projects should be signiﬁcantly reduced from setbacks adopted for wind projects. 
•Waste Generation/Spills: o Solar panel equipment does not utilize lubricates or c oolants, 
resulting in minimal waste/recycling. Waste management requirements should follow 
applicable existing law. •Wildlife/Habitat Impacts: o Solar projects have minimal impacts on

<!-- page 1177 -->
13 
 
wildlife and SB Energy’s project incorporates wildlife and livestock corridors  as well as 
fencing gaps to allow passage through the project. •Noise: o Solar panels do not produce 
noise, and any minimal noise is usually isolated to electrical inverter oper ations or site 
maintenance work activities, reducing setback requirements related to noise. •Safety: o 
Solar projects have limited moving parts and are low to the ground eliminating overhead 
hazards resulting in reduced setback needs due to safety concerns . We ask the Board of 
Supervisors to consider these signiﬁcant community beneﬁts and key differences when 
developing a solar ordinance. SB Energy is happy to provide any feedback or expertise in 
drafting the solar ordinance and looks forward to continued coordination on solar energy 
development in Navajo County. Thank you.

LETTER: First, we thank you for hosting the previous listening sessions. They were very well-
organized and productive. It was refreshing to hear how many constituents are in favor of 
renewables. Second, Aztec would like to reiterate its opposition to the revisions to the wind 
ordinance that seemed to be suggested by County staff in the listening sessions. Increased 
setbacks from residences and non-participating landowners and new setbacks from 
incorporated areas and National Forest land are changes for the sake of change. In our 
opinion, they are being suggested to placate a loud minority… a minority whose primary 
concern (whether or not stated) is keeping a viewshed permanently unaltered. Aztec has 
been a responsible steward of land in Navajo County since 1 884. Time and time again, our 
company chose not to subdivide and not to sell - while many others did (which they had every 
right to do). Now, Aztec is choosing to develop some of its land (which it has every right to 
do) in a sustainable, responsible manne r. Given that Navajo County's existing wind 
ordinance is one of the most stringent in the state (if not the country), we urge that Planning 
and Zoning staff and the Board of Supervisors refrain from making any substantial revisions 
to it. We also ask, as t he County evaluates its wind energy ordinance, that it weigh what I 
would term 'on the ground' circumstances, as follows: 
• The Wind Resource 
Parts (but by no means all) of Navajo County's landscape have a substantial and 
economic wind resource - meaning enough wind enough of the year to justify the 
enormous investment to create a wind energy project. Projects will ipso facto go to 
where such re sources exist. Overly restrictive wind energy zoning limitations will 
inadvertently make either some or a lot of that wind resource unavailable, to the 
economic detriment, for sure, of a landowner in such an area who wishes to 
participate, but also to the detriment of Navajo County in the form of lost property 
taxes, lost employment opportunities for its residents, and lost follow-on beneﬁts to 
numerous local businesses from whom you heard during your listening sessions. A 
wind resource above one's property is a property right, and unreasonable denial of its 
use is the denial of that property right. 
• Existing Ultra-High Voltage Transmission 
The area where our land is located (and elsewhere in central Navajo County) is cris-
crossed with, by my count, some 130 miles of ultra-high voltage power lines, which, 
in themselves, amount to a multi -billion dollar 'resource' paid for by APS and SRP 
ratepayers (including the residents of Navajo County) over many years. In addition to 
the wind resource discussed above, wind (and solar) energy developers are attracted 
to our area because there are, or will be, substantial 'vacancies' in transmission 
capacity use which the renewable projects seeking zoning approval from Navajo 
County, and the utilities who buy their output, look to make use of. It is, in our opinion, 
well beyond the proper zoning purview of Navajo County to, by overly restrictive 
zoning conditions, deny use of this transmission 'resource' to the detriment of all of 
Navajo County, and, indeed our state. Additionally, if as we believe the fundamental 
objection to wind energy development is viewshed alteration, the existing viewshed - 
the one we take for granted because it is already there - is already altered by literally 
a forest of high voltage transmission lines and towers. 
• Forest Setbacks

<!-- page 1180 -->
16 
 
We believe it is unwise to adopt a setback standard from National Forest boundaries 
(as opposed to inholdings). The point where National Forest land in Navajo County 
meets its north boundary is characterized by lower elevation trees (mostly cedar and 
some, but not a lot, of jack pine), poor soils, de -minimus watering places, lack of 
vegetative undergrowth (both of which mean it is beneﬁcial only for transitory 
wildlife), and negligible recreation value. Further, inasmuch as National Forest land 
can't be de veloped, such setbacks are of no beneﬁt to the National Forest land the 
setback purports to 'protect' . Regarding solar, Aztec is not opposed to the 
implementation of a formal ordinance governing solar development and 
construction. We look forward to learning more about the content of said ordinance 
in the coming weeks and hope that it closely resembles the conditions currently 
imposed under the existing special use permit process. 
We so appreciate you taking the time to consider our feedback.

JOTFORM (1): Property devaluation due to Wind & Solar Farms Data The impact of wind and 
solar farms on property values in rural areas has been a topic of signiﬁcant concern. Recent 
studies and real estate data have shed some light some on this issue, revealing that the 
presence of these costly eye soars of so called renewable energy installations can and do 
indeed have a negative effect on nearby property values as well as real property that is within 
eye site.  Wind and solar farms, while championed for their over inﬂated and often 
misrepresented environmental beneﬁts , disrupt the natural beauty that draws people to 
rural areas—think rolling hills, open ﬁelds, or forested vistas, think of the beauty of the White 
Mountains, replaced or interrupted by towering twirling turbines, blinking lights or sprawling 
light glaring, heat generating solar panels. Studies and simple anecdotal evidence suggest 
that proximity to these installations can lower property values, primarily due to diminished 
visual appeal, noise (in the case of wind turbines), and total loss of tranquility. Not to 
mention the killing off of birds, that includes Bald & Golden Eagles, bats and insects, greatly 
disrupting the natural order of things. For example, research on wind farms has shown mixed 
results, but some studies, like one from the Journal of Real Estate Research (2016), found

<!-- page 1187 -->
23 
 
that properties within a few miles of turbines can see value drops of 5 -15%, depending on 
factors like distance, density of turbines, and the original appeal of the area. Solar farms, 
though quieter, can still transform large swathes of land into what some  describe as an 
"industrial eyesore, " potentially deterring buyers who prioritize scenic views. The mechanism 
here is straightforward: rural properties often trade on their seclusion, natural beauty, and 
recreational potential. When industrialization encroaches—especially in areas marketed as 
pristine—demand will soften. Buyers seeking a peaceful retreat will look elsewhere, 
shrinking the pool of potential purchasers and pushing prices down. This effect is more 
pronounced in regions where tourism or second-home markets (e.g., vacation cottages) 
bolster property values, as visual degradation directly undercuts those industries.  Farmers 
hosting turbines or panels might see a steady income, providing the Wind or Solar 
Corporation make money off the units, and i f they don’t go bankrupt and abandon the site. 
These leases only beneﬁt the land owner, and there are no guarantees on most of these 
leases. This greatly hurts and disturbs all the other property owners in the surrounding areas, 
for miles around on many different levels. Resentment is a huge factor that these 
communities' face, and you BoS, should be acutely aware of it, as a lot of this resentment is 
directed at you for making these Special Use Permits available to these Corporations that 
don’t care about what is important to our community. The community is devastated at these 
future catastrophic changes in our landscapes, our wild life, our way of life. This is another 
huge factor in depressing the real estate market and our economy. Tourism-dependent spots 
like the White Mountains are devalued more and take longer to sell because of the impact of 
being with in eye site, of what once was a pristine landscape, that has been turn into an 
industrialized eye soar, that has become permanently  “Spoiled” .  Data Wind Farms  
Research indicates that wind turbines lead to a decrease in property values, particularly for 
homes in closer proximity to these installations. The extent of this impact varies depending 
on factors such as distance, visibility, and the size of the wind farm: Properties within 1 mile 
of wind turbines have experienced average value decreases of 7%, with houses in rural areas 
seeing drops of up to 23% [1] Some studies have found that homes within 1.2 miles of wind 
turbines can see value reductions ranging from 25% to 40% [1][2] The effect of wind turbines 
on property values can extend up to 5 to 10 miles from the installation site[1]And extend all 
the way to “Within Eye Site” . Example is the eye sores now seen from Show Low on 260 
looking towards Snow Flake. The complete ruin of the aesthetic charm of the expansive 
landscape. Data Solar Farms In rural areas, solar farms DO devalue nearby real property. 
However, The data found on the impact Solar Farms have on real property values have mostly 
been done by the building Solar Corporations or a hired by them, and not by independent 
studies and therefore are deemed biases and unreliable. So simply based on Location, 
Location, Location: as the main moto in selling real property: Lets visit some realities that 
are directly in front of our faces: Rural settings are more sensitive to devaluing due to their 
reliance on landscape and agricultural identity. Rural property values often hinge on open 
space, scenic views, and agricultural use. A solar farm swaps ﬁelds or forests for panels and 
fencing, which can feel like an industrial intrusion. Think of a 100-acre cornﬁeld turning into

future value.### Inﬂation Calculation The formula for future value wi th compound interest 
(or inﬂation) is: 
\[ FV = PV \times (1 + r)^n \]Where: 
- \( FV \) = Future Value (what we need in 20 years) 
- \( PV \) = Present Value (today’s cost, $1 billion)

<!-- page 1196 -->

- \( r \) = Annual inﬂation rate (0.03 or 3%) 
- \( n \) = Number of years (20) 
Plugging in the numbers: 
\[ FV = 1,000,000,000 \times (1 + 0.03)^{20} \] 
\[ FV = 1,000,000,000 \times (1.03)^{20} \] 
\[ FV = 1,000,000,000 \times 1.806111 \] 
\[ FV \approx 1,806,111,000 \] 
So, after 20 years at 3% annual inﬂation, the $1 billion needed today would grow to 
approximately **$1.806 billion** . This means the escrow account should be funded with at 
least $1.806 billion upfront to ensure it covers the inﬂated decommissioning cost s in 20 
years (assuming no interest accrual—just inﬂation protection). For simplicity, I’ll round this 
to **$1.81 billion** in the ordinance and include a periodic review clause to adjust for actual 
inﬂation trends.---### Revised County Ordinance No. [In sert Number]#### An Ordinance

ﬂexibility to choose between these approaches based on county preferences. ### Inﬂation 
Scenarios. Using the same future value formula ( \( FV = PV \times (1 + r)^n \ )), with \( PV = 
$1,000,000,000 \) (for 200 windmills) and \( n = 20 \):  
**2% Annual Inﬂation**: 
\[ FV = 1,000,000,000 \times (1.02)^{20} \] 
\[ FV = 1,000,000,000 \times 1.485947 \] 
\[ FV \approx 1,485,947,000 \] 
Total needed: ~**$1.486 billion** (rounded). 
 **3% Annual Inﬂation** (from previous calculation): 
\[ FV \approx 1,806,111,000 \] 
Total needed: ~**$1.81 billion** . 
**4% Annual Inﬂation**: 
\[ FV = 1,000,000,000 \times (1.04)^{20} \] 
\[ FV = 1,000,000,000 \times 2.191123 \] 
\[ FV \approx 2,191,123,000 \] 
Total needed: ~**$2.191 billion** (rounded). 
### Interest Earnings Assumption. If the escrow account earns interest at a rate equal to 
inﬂation (e.g., 3% interest matching 3% inﬂation), the future value of the initial $1 billion 
would grow to match the inﬂated decommissioning cost without additional upfront funding:  
At 3% interest: \( 1,000,000,000 \times (1.03)^{20} \approx $1.81 billion \), covering the cost.  
This assumes the interest rate remains stable and matches inﬂation exactly, which is 
optimistic but possible with a well -managed account. To balance realism and ﬂexibility, I’ll 
revise the ordinance to allow the county to choose an inﬂation rate between 2% and 4% 
(defaulting to 3%) and offer an interest -accrual option as an alternative to full upfront 
funding. ### Revised County Ordinance No. [Insert Number] 
#### An Ordinance Establishing Financial Assurance Requirements for Wind Energy 
Projects 
**WHEREAS** , the construction of wind energy facilities, including windmills, represents a 
signiﬁcant investment with long -term environmental and economic impacts on [County 
Name]; and 
**WHEREAS** , each windmill is estimated to cost approximately $5,000,000 to construct, 
with a 200 -windmill project totaling approximately $1,000,000,000 in initial capital 
expenditure; and 
**WHEREAS** , the costs of decommissioning, dismantling, and restoring or remediating 
wind energy project sites are estimated to be equivalent to the initial construction costs, 
requiring an additional $1,000,000,000 for a 200-windmill project; and 
**WHEREAS** , the operational lifespan of such wind energy facilities is typically 20 years, 
during which inﬂation may increase decommissioning costs, with estimates ranging from 
$1,486,000,000 at 2% annual inﬂation to $2,191,000,000 at 4% annual inﬂatio n, and 
approximately $1,810,000,000 at 3% annual inﬂation; and

<!-- page 1199 -->
35 
 
**WHEREAS** , it is in the public interest to ensure that sufficient ﬁnancial resources are 
available to cover the full lifecycle costs of wind energy projects, including decommissioning 
and site remediation, without imposing future burdens on taxpayers or landowners; 
**NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED** by the NAVAJO COUNTY Board of Commissioners 
as follows: 
#### Section 1: Purpose 
The purpose of this ordinance is to establish ﬁnancial assurance requirements for wind 
energy projects to guarantee that adequate funds are available for the construction, 
operation, decommissioning, and site restoration of wind energy facilities within NAVAJO 
COUNTY . 
#### Section 2: Deﬁnitions 
- **Wind Energy Facility**: Any installation consisting of one or more wind turbines or 
windmills designed to generate electricity from wind power. 
- **Decommissioning**: The process of dismantling and removing wind energy facilities at 
the end of their operational life, including site restoration and remediation to pre -
construction conditions. 
- **Escrow Account**: A dedicated ﬁnancial account established to hold funds for the 
purpose of covering decommissioning and site restoration costs. 
#### Section 3: Financial Assurance Requirement 
1. **Escrow Account Establishment**: Any entity seeking to construct a wind energy facility 
within NAVAJO COUNTY shall establish an escrow account with a ﬁnancial institution 
approved by the County Treasurer. 
2. **Base Funding Amount**: The escrow account shall be funded at a rate of one dollar ($1) 
for every dollar ($1) of estimated construction costs for the wind energy facility, as 
determined by a detailed cost estimate submitted by the applicant and approve d by the 
County Planning Department. For example, a facility with 200 windmills, each costing 
$5,000,000, shall require a base amount of $1,000,000,000. 
3. **Inﬂation Adjustment Options**: 
- **Option A: Full Upfront Funding**: The escrow account shall include an inﬂation 
adjustment based on a projected annual inﬂation rate between 2% and 4%, as determined 
by the County Treasurer (defaulting to 3% unless otherwise speciﬁed). For a 20 -year period 
at 3%, the total funding requirement shall be approximately 1.81 ti mes the base amount 
(e.g., $1,810,000,000 for a 200-windmill project). At 2%, this shall be 1.486 times the base 
amount (e.g., $1,486,000,000), and at 4%, 2.191 times the base amount (e.g., 
$2,191,000,000). 
- **Option B: Interest-Accrual Funding**: Alternatively, the applicant may fund the escrow 
account with the base amount only (e.g., $1,000,000,000 for 200 windmills), provided the 
account is invested in a secure, interest -bearing instrument approved by the  County 
Treasurer, with an expected annual return equal to or exceeding the chosen inﬂation rate 
(defaulting to 3%). The applicant must demonstrate that the account will accrue sufficient 
funds to meet the inﬂation-adjusted decommissioning cost after 20 years. 
4. **Periodic Review**: Every ﬁve (5) years, the County Treasurer shall review the escrow 
account balance against updated inﬂation projections (based on the Consumer Price Index 
or another index designated by the County) and the performance of any intere st-bearing

<!-- page 1200 -->
36 
 
investments. If the account is deemed insufficient, the applicant shall contribute additional 
funds within 90 days to meet the projected need. 
5. **Proof of Funding**: Prior to the issuance of any construction permits, the applicant shall 
provide proof of the fully funded escrow account under Option A or a certiﬁed investment 
plan under Option B, veriﬁed by the ﬁnancial institution holding the funds. 
#### Section 4: Use of Escrow Funds 
1. Funds in the escrow account shall be reserved exclusively for the costs of 
decommissioning, dismantling, and restoring or remediating the wind energy facility site to 
its pre-construction condition, as determined by the County Planning Department. 
2. Withdrawals from the escrow account shall be permitted only upon approval by the 
County Board of Commissioners and shall be contingent upon the submission of a 
decommissioning plan meeting county standards. 
#### Section 5: Enforcement 
1. Failure to establish or maintain the required escrow account, including inﬂation-adjusted 
contributions or interest -accrual performance, shall result in the denial or revocation of 
construction permits and may subject the applicant to ﬁnes not exceedi ng [$X] per day of 
noncompliance. 
2. The County reserves the right to assume control of the escrow account and undertake 
decommissioning activities if the operator fails to do so within [X] months of the facility 
reaching the end of its operational life. 
#### Section 6: Effective Date 
This ordinance shall take effect [insert date] and apply to all wind energy projects proposed 
or constructed thereafter. 
--- 
### Key Adjustments: 1. **Flexibility**: The ordinance now offers a range of inﬂation rates 
(2% to 4%) and two funding options: full upfront payment or interest -accrual with the base 
amount. This accommodates different economic assumptions and develop er preferences.  
2. **Realism**: The interest-accrual option assumes a stable return, but the periodic review 
ensures the county isn’t left short if investments underperform. 3. **Clarity**: Speciﬁc 
dollar amounts are provided for a 200 -windmill project a t each inﬂation rate, making the 
requirements transparent. To adjust the default inﬂation rate, reﬁne the interest -accrual 
rules (e.g., specify a minimum return). NAVAJO COUNTY will reﬁne the ordinance by 
adjusting the default inﬂation rate and enhancing the interest-accrual rules. For this revision, 
shift the default inﬂation rate from 3% to **2.5%** as a middle ground between the 2% and 
4% scenarios, reﬂecting a cautious but not overly conservative estimate. Also to specify a 
**minimum interest ret urn** of 2.5% for the interest -accrual option, with stricter 
requirements to ensure the account grows sufficiently, including a contingency buffer. ###

\[ FV = 1,000,000,000 \times (1.025)^{20} \] 
\[ FV = 1,000,000,000 \times 1.638616 \] 
\[ FV \approx 1,638,616,000 \] 
Total needed: ~**$1.639 billion** (rounded).

NAME: Nina Triolo

COMMENT: 
HEBER: Nina emphasized the need to protect future generations by requiring wind and solar 
farm developers to set aside a cash deposit for decommissioning costs. She proposed that 
every approved project establishes an escrow or bond amount, approximately 1.8 times the 
estimated cost—generally $2-3 million per wind farm —subject to review and adjustment 
every ﬁve years. Tri olo cited examples of ﬁnancial burdens placed on taxpayers due to 
inadequate decommissioning funds, including Minnesota's Palmers Creek wind facility, 
where cost estimates failed to account for inﬂation and disposal challenges. She also 
highlighted Texas, which lacks uniform decommissioning requirements, leaving rural 
counties vulnerable to cleanup costs if developers abandon sites. A failed 2019 Texas bill 
attempted to mandate ﬁnancial assurances, underscoring the risk that taxpayers could be 
left footing multimillion-dollar decommissioning bills. She concluded by stressing the need 
for regulatory foresight, skilled labor, and ﬁnancial safeguards in Navajo County’s renewable 
energy policies. 
 
JOTFORM (1): I am proposing Ordinances that every approved wind or solar farm needs to 
set aside a cash deposit in an escrow account to cover the full cost of decommissioning and 
disposal after 30 years. This deposit should be about 1.7 times the estimated cost, 
reasonably and generally $2.5 to $3.5 million per wind turbine. To keep up with inﬂation and 
other changes, the amount will be reviewed and adjusted every 5 years. The 
decommissioning of wind and solar farms has emerged as a ﬁnancial burden for taxpayers 
and local governments in several regions, often due to inadequate cost projections, lack of 
regulatory foresight, or insufficient ﬁnancial assurances from developers.  I'm going to share 
a few documented examples and contexts where this issue has been observed or is 
anticipated based on current trends and policies as of March 25, 2025. In the United States 
In Minnesota - Wind Turbine Decommissioning Costs: Xcel Energy, a major utility in 
Minnesota, estimated in 2019 that decommissioning a single wind turbine co sts 
approximately $532,000 (in 2019 dollars), with the Palmer’s Creek Wind Facility (18 turbines) 
projected at $7.4 million total. These estimates were conservative and did not fully account

<!-- page 1216 -->
52 
 
for inﬂation, evolving disposal challenges like (non-recyclable ﬁberglass blades), or site -
speciﬁc restoration needs like deep foundation removal. If developers fail to set aside 
sufficient funds —often only 2 -3% of capital costs annually —local governmen ts or we 
taxpayers could be left to cover shortfalls, especially for older projects permitted without 
robust decommissioning bonds. Texas has a Lack of Statewide Standards: Texas, a leader in 
wind energy, has NO uniform statewide decommissioning requirements, leaving it to 
counties to negotiate with developers. A 2019 legislative attempt (House Bill 2845) to 
mandate ﬁnancial assurances for wind farm decommissioning failed. Without such 
mandates, rural counties risk bearing cleanup costs if developers abandon unproﬁtable 
sites. For instance, the Texas Public Policy Foundation warned in 2021 that 
decommissioning an average solar farm could exceed $1 million, a cost that could fall on 
taxpayers if developers default, given the rapid proliferation of projects and reliance on 
federal subsidies like the Production Tax Credit. These huge turbines and solar farms require 
special equipment (500 ft cranes) and highly skilled teams for the decommissioning and 
restoration processes. These should be included along with the ﬁnancial component in the 
new ordinances. THANK YOU, Nina Triolo 
 
JOTFORM (2): I have more examples of decommissioning requirements and projected costs. 
Questions: Where are the accountability factors for the oldest wind farm in Arizona, Pink 
Cliffs? Has anyone on the board or commission shared Pink Cliffs promises and production 
efficiency? Decommissioning and disposing of a 600-foot wind turbine—a massive structure 
likely referring to something like a 3-5 MW onshore turbine— involves signiﬁcant costs, and 
whether $5 to $7 million is enough depends on a variety of factors, including location, labor 
rates, disposal methods, and site restoration requirements. Let’s break it down. A 600 -foot 
turbine, assuming total height including the blade tip, typically has a tower height of around 
300-400 feet and blades extending another 200- 300 feet. These are industrial -scale 
machines weighing 200 -400 tons total, with components like steel towers (150 -250 tons), 
ﬁberglass blades (15 -20 tons each, often three per turbine), and a nacelle (housing the 
generator, gearbox, etc., about 50 -100 tons). Decommissioning involves dismantling, 
transporting, and disposing or recycling these parts, plus restoring the site. **Cost 
Breakdown:** 1. **Dismantling**: Requires heavy cranes (e.g., a 600 -ton crane), rigging 
crews, and safety measures. Crane  rental alone can run $50,000 -$100,000 per week, and 
disassembly might take 1 -2 weeks. Labor and equipment costs typically range $200,000 -
$500,000 per turbine, depending on site access and complexity. 2. **Transportation**: 
Moving hundreds of tons of mater ial—especially oversized blades (up to 200 feet long) —
needs specialized trucks and permits. Hauling costs can hit $100,000 -$300,000, higher if 
the site’s remote or roads need upgrades. 3. **Disposal/Recycling**: Steel and copper (from 
the tower and nacelle) are recyclable, offsetting some costs—scrap steel fetches $200-$300 
per ton, potentially netting $30,000 -$75,000. But blades are a problem: made of ﬁberglass 
and resin, they’re tough to recycle. Landﬁlling costs $50-$100 per ton, so three 20-ton blades 
could be $3,000-$6,000, but many regions now restrict this, pushing toward expensive 
alternatives like shredding or incineration ($200-$400 per ton, or $12,000-$24,000 total). 
Recycling tech (e.g., pyrolysis) exists but isn’t widespread and jacks up costs further. 4. 
**Site Restoration**: Removing the concrete foundation (500-1,000 tons) and regrading the

<!-- page 1217 -->
53 
 
land can cost $250,000 -$1 million, depending on depth and environmental regulations. 
Some sites leave foundations buried to save money, but stricter rules might demand full 
removal. 5. **Permitting and Admin**: Fees, environmental studies, and legal overhead add 
$50,000-$200,000. **Total Estimates**: Industry data varies widely. A 2021 National 
Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) study pegs decommissioning at $200,000 -$500,000 
per MW for onshore turbines, so a 3 MW turbine might run $600,000 -$1.5 million. However, 
real-world examples —like a Texas project in 2023—reported $1.5 -$2 million per turbine 
when including full foundation removal and blade disposal challenges. Offshore turbines 
(not your case) can hit $5 million+, but onshore costs rarely approach that  unless logistics 
are brutal (e.g., mountainous terrain, no nearby recycling). For one 600-foot turbine: A high-
end estimate might reach $2-$3 million if everything goes wrong: maxed-out labor, long-haul 
transport, and zero scrap value. Your range suggests either a misunderstanding of scale (e.g., 
conﬂating one turbine with a whole wind farm) or extreme contingency padding. A small wind 
farm of 5-10 such turbines could hit $5-$7 million total, but for a single unit, $1-$3 million.  
Please reassess the projected farms costs of decommissioning and make sure a bond is 
posted so county tax payers are not left footing the enormous bills for decommissioning.  
Thank you.

Who Decommissioning costs, including dismantling turbines and restoring sites, were often 
underestimated in initial projections, which focused on installation and operation RATHER

county, especially any wind farms.  There are already windfarms within the county which

studies already show the negative effects these windfarms have on our environment and as 
a voting tax payer and property owner, I will not support any politicians or council members 
that promote such developments.

NAME: Jordy Fuentes 
CITY: Phoenix 
PLATFORM: Show Low Listening Session 
COMMENT: 
Jordy Fuentes, a longtime Navajo County resident and executive director of the Arizona 
Power Authority, addressed the need for balanced energy solutions. His agency wholesales 
power to rural areas, including Apache Electric and irrigation districts. Drawin g on his legal 
background, Fuentes noted that while the county cannot outright ban energy projects due to 
legal constraints, zoning regulations can help address community concerns. He 
emphasized the importance of diversifying power sources, especially with coal plants 
shutting down and threatening the local tax base and jobs. Fuentes advocated proactive 
planning to replace the economic beneﬁts of large coal plants by encouraging smaller 
energy projects that collectively sustain the community’s long-term viability. He stressed the 
need for thoughtful zoning and continued dialogue to achieve a balanced energy approach. 
 
NAME: Cory Johnson 
CITY: Snowﬂake 
PLATFORM: Show Low Listening Session 
COMMENT: 
Cory, a lifelong resident of Snowﬂake, expressed his gratitude for the opportunities provided 
by his community, despite the challenges of limited job availability. As a rancher, he 
acknowledged the difficulties of maintaining a ranch with limited resources and the impact 
of power plant closures, particularly the sadness surrounding the closing of Cholla. Cory, 
who is also the Snowﬂake School Board President, highlighted the ﬁnancial strain on the 
district due to its status as one of the poorest in Arizona, requiring bonds to fund educational 
needs. He emphasized how wind and solar projects could help alleviate the tax burden on 
individual homeowners, contributing to local schools and providing much-needed jobs in 
the area.

<!-- page 1220 -->
56 
 
 
NAME: John Glitsos 
CITY: Lakeside 
PLATFORM: Show Low Listening Session 
COMMENT: 
John, president of the White Mountain Nature Center and co-founder of Land on Sky Wildlife 
Experiences, addressed concerns about wind farms killing birds, particularly bald eagles 
and raptors. He shared statistics showing that for every bird killed by a wind turbine, 10,000 
are killed by cats left outside, 2,500 by collisions with building windows, and 307 by 
poisoning from rat poison. He emphasized that these factors cause far more bird deaths than 
wind turbines and urged the public to take responsibility by keeping cats indoors, placing 
decals on windows, and addressing poisoning issues before blaming wind farms. He 
encouraged action on these preventable issues, which can be controlled by individuals. 
 
NAME: Brandon Perkins 
CITY: Show Low 
PLATFORM: Show Low Listening Session 
COMMENT: 
Brandon Perkins, owner of Perkins Cinders and Perkins Aggregates, shared his family's long 
history in Show Low, recalling how they used to deal with heavy snowfalls in the area. He 
expressed his gratitude for the opportunities provided by his company, whic h employs 
around 150 people and has contributed signiﬁcantly to the local economy by selling sand 
and gravel and providing trucking services. Brandon emphasized his deep love for wildlife 
and concern for the environment but acknowledged the economic beneﬁ ts of local 
industries, which have supported various sectors such as realtors, ranchers, cafes, well 
drillers, and more. He concluded by highlighting the widespread positive impact these 
industries have had on the community and the state, feeding families and providing work 
opportunities. 
 
NAME: Roger L. Gorres 
CITY: Heber 
PLATFORM: Heber Listening Session 
COMMENT: 
Roger urged the county to consider increasing the setback distance for electric wind 
turbines, proposing a range of ﬁve to seven miles from the nearest residence not on the 
landowner’s property. They advised against adopting the extreme 12 -mile restrictio n in 
Arizona’s HB 2223, citing an article stating it would make Arizona the most restrictive state 
for wind power and eliminate 90% of suitable land for development. They also emphasized 
the visual impact, noting that proposed turbines could reach 800 feet—equivalent to an 80-
story building. Lastly, they suggested aligning setbacks with international standards from 
countries like Norway and Australia, which have adjusted distances based on experience. 
 
NAME: Matt Kesler

<!-- page 1221 -->
57 
 
CITY: Phoenix 
PLATFORM: Heber Listening Session & Joseph City Listening Session 
COMMENT: 
HEBER: Matt, Director of Solar Technology at OMCO Solar, spoke about advancements in 
solar energy and its environmental impact. While not advocating for or against speciﬁc 
ordinances, he highlighted improvements in solar technology that reduce environmental 
harm. He discussed agrivoltaics, which combines solar panels with agriculture by allowing 
grazing underneath or enhancing crops through strategic shading. He noted that modern 
solar installations require less land grading, minimizing disruption to wildlife and vegetation. 
Additionally, advancements in recycling allow solar modules and batteries to be largely 
recyclable, with companies like First Solar leading in this area. Kessler emphasized that 
today’s solar plants are more environmentally friendly than those of the past and offered his 
expertise and resources to assist Navajo County in making informed decisions. 
 
JOSEPH CITY: Matt explained that while his company does not develop solar power plants, 
it manufactures mounting systems for solar panels. He acknowledged concerns raised in a 
previous meeting about the environmental impact of solar energy, which surprised him, as 
he has long believed solar has the lowest environmental impact when generating energy. 
However, he noted that industry practices have evolved signiﬁcantly over the years. Unlike 
in the past, modern solar projects now use mounting systems that conform to natu ral land 
contours, minimizing grading and disruption to vegetation and wildlife. Additionally, 
advancements in solar technology allow for cost-effective refurbishing of older solar farms, 
replacing worn parts to restore efficiency with minimal waste. He em phasized that most 
outdated materials, such as glass, can now be recycled, reducing environmental impact. 
Lastly, he highlighted his company’s collaboration with the Arizona Solar Energy Student 
Association as a valuable resource for sharing information and addressing concerns about 
solar energy.

He mentioned that his father -in-law, a local rancher, signed an agreement to explore wind 
energy, which has provided ﬁnancial beneﬁts to the ranch. While he remains neutral on 
some aspects, he emphasized the importance of using common sense in decision-making 
and ensuring that coal plants are not shut down without a reliable replacement in place.

NAME: Autumn Johnson 
CITY: Scottsdale 
PLATFORM: Joseph City Listening Session 
COMMENT: 
Autumn Johnson, Executive Director of the Arizona Solar Energy Industries Association 
(ARISEIA), discussed energy policy and the economic impacts of renewable projects. 
ARISEIA has worked on similar ordinances across Arizona and emphasized the importance 
of all -source requests for proposals (RFPs), which allow different energy resources to 
compete based on factors like cost, geographic diversity, and grid reliability. She shared 
ﬁndings from an economic impact assessment conducted by Arizona-based ﬁrm Ell iot 
Pollock, showing that a 200 MW solar plus battery storage project in Navajo County would 
create 285 jobs, generate $682,000 in construction taxes, and contribute $18.7 million over 
its lifetime. A similar wind assessment for Coconino County projected $ 12.4 million in tax 
revenues and $862.5 million in total economic activity. Johnson highlighted additional 
community beneﬁts that can be incorporated into procurement processes and pointed to 
various resources, such as the International City/County Manage ment Association’s 
SolSmart program, the American Clean Power Association, and the National Fire Protection 
Association, which provide technical assistance and model ordinances. She encouraged the 
county to consider different requirements for solar and wind due to differences in height and 
offered ARISEIA’s support throughout the process.

NAME: Ronald Pedersen 
CITY: Lakeside

Under the current circumstances, it's apparent that the focus for renewable energy in Navajo 
County should be on biomass energy generation.  Here are the facts: 1) The Apache

NAME: Rebecca Heward 
CITY:  
PLATFORM: Email 
COMMENT: 
Dear County Managers, I am writing to express a growing concern regarding the recent push 
for wind and solar farms in our area, speciﬁcally in relation to the use and transport of lithium 
batteries. While we recognize the importance of pursuing renewable energy, it is crucial that 
we also consider the potential safety hazards associated with these technologies. There 
have already been incidents involving lithium battery accidents on highways and within 
populated areas, which raise signiﬁcant concerns about the dangers they pose in the event 
of a ﬁre, explosion, or toxic release. These risks are particularly alarming given our region’s 
exposure to high winds and the proximity of major transportation routes like I -40. In light of 
these concerns, we strongly urge Navajo County to adopt a minimum ﬁve-mile setback from 
incorporated areas when rezoning for such facilities. While this measure does not eliminate

We deserve to have air that is easy to breathe and water that isn’t full of oil. Renewable

NAME: Tim Grubbs 
CITY: Show Low 
PLATFORM: Online Survey 
COMMENT: 
Thanks for this opportunity to provide input on Navajo County's renewable energy ordinance. 
I'm a Navajo County resident, and I'd like to see more renewable energy sited to meet energy 
demand. A good ordinance should: 1) Enable development near existing energy 
infrastructure like transmission lines and substations. To do this, it needs to be free of caps 
on acreage or other restrictive conditions or if caps are opted for, they should be reasonable 
to allow enough projects to fully utilize the existing energy infrastructure in the area. 2) Look 
after community interests. To do this, the ordinance application process should build in early 
and frequent consultation with stakeholders, such as wildlife agencies (USFWS, Game and 
Fish), Tribal communities and agencies, historic preservation off icers, and the local 
community. 3) Treat solar and wind development fairly. The default should be to match 
existing underlying zoning requirements. Too often in local renewable energy ordinances we 
see requirements unnecessarily applied to renewable energy that don't apply to other uses 
with more negative impacts on the community. 4) Be based on science and evidence. A well-
researched science and evidence-based approach will recognize solar and wind as largely 
passive uses. For purely health and safety purposes, reasonable setbacks for solar should 
be 150 to 300 ft for solar. It sho uld be ¾ mile to 1 mile for wind. Extremely large setbacks 
could result in a de facto moratorium on wind and solar development and prevent the type 
of renewable energy development necessary to meet increasing demand for electricity in the 
state.

RESOLUTION ____-25
A RESOLUTION OF THE NAVAJO COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS ADOPTING
AN AMENDMENT TO THE NAVAJO COUNTY ZONING ORDINANCE
WHEREAS, Planning & Development Services Staff has recommended the amendment
of the Navajo County Zoning Ordinance, Ordinance No. Z90-1; and
WHEREAS, a duly noticed public hearing on said amendments was held by the Navajo
County Planning and Zoning Commission on June 19th, 2025; and
WHEREAS, the Navajo County Board of Supervisors after considering the testimony
and other evidence presented at the hearing, as well as the recommendations of Staff, found that
the Zoning Ordinance Amendment is consistent with the public health, safety, and general welfare
and should be approved as set forth herein; and
NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED  the Board of Supervisors hereby
adopts in whole the proposed changes and amendments to the attached draft of the Navajo County
Zoning Ordinance:
SECTION 1. The amended Navajo County Zoning Ordinance shall contain the following articles:
ARTICLE 1 – TITLE AND PURPOSE
ARTICLE 2 – ZONING DISTRICT
ARTICLE 3 – A-GENERAL ZONING DISTRICT
ARTICLE 4 – RURAL ZONING DISTRICTS (RU)
ARTICLE 5 – SINGLE-FAMILY ZONING DISTRICTS (R1)
ARTICLE 6 – MULTI-FAMILY ZONING DISTRICTS (R)
ARTICLE 7 – COMMERCIAL-RESIDENTIAL ZONING DISTRICT (C-R)
ARTICLE 8 – INDUSTRIAL ZONING DISTRICTS (IND)
ARTICLE 9 – SPECIAL DEVELOPMENT ZONE (SD)
ARTICLE 10 – ADULT ORIENTED BUSINESSES (AOBs)
ARTICLE 11 – MARIJUANA FACILITIES
ARTICLE 12 – RENEWABLE ENERGY
ARTICLE 13 – WIRELESS COMMUNICATION FACLITIES
ARTICLE 14 – HEARING PROCESSES
ARTICLE 15 – RECREATIONAL VEHICLE PLACEMENT (RV)
ARTICLE 16 – PARKING
ARTICLE 17 – SIGNS
ARTICLE 18 – OUTDOOR LIGHTING
ARTICLE 19 – GENERAL PROVISIONS

<!-- page 1229 -->
Navajo County - For Official Use Only
ARTICLE 20 – NON-CONFORMING USES
ARTICLE 21 – ADMINISTRATION, VIOLATION, ENFORCEMENT, AND PENALTY
ARTICLE 22 – NUISANCES AND ABATEMENT
ARTICLE 23 - DEFINITIONS
SECTION 2. Separability
Should any Article, Section, or regulation of this Ordinance be declared by the courts to be
unconstitutional or invalid, such decision shall not affect the validity of the Ordinance as a whole,
or any portion thereof other than the Article, Section, or regulation so declared to be
unconstitutional or invalid.
SECTION 3. Repeal of Conflicting Ordinance
All Ordinances or portions of Ordinances in conflict with this Ordinance, or inconsistent with the
regulations of this Ordinance, are hereby repealed to the extent necessary to give this Ordinance
full force and effect.
SECTION 3. Clerical Corrections
The County Clerk is hereby authorized to correct typographical and grammatical errors, as
well as errors of wording and punctuation, as necessary related to this ordinance as amended
herein, and to make formatting changes needed for purposes of clarity and form, or
consistency, within thirty (30) days following adoption by the Board of Supervisors.
SECTION 4. Effective Date
In order to preserve Public Peace, Health, and Safety, it is necessary that this Ordinance become
immediately operative. It is therefore declared to be an emergency measure, to take effect
immediately upon its passage by the Board of Supervisors, pursuant to A.R.S. § 11-813(G).
PASSED AND ADOPTED by the Navajo County Board of Supervisors by a vote of
_____ yeas and ______ nays on this 24th day of June 2025.
NAVAJO COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS
By ________________________________________

<!-- page 1252 -->
PROPOSED UPDATES TO ORDINANCE
• Combine general development standards for solar and wind, under Renewable Energy Generation Facilities.
• Add clause to allow for the use of Development Agreements in-lieu of, or in combination with, Special Use Permits.
• Add in preferred criteria and performance standards for renewable projects.
• Add stronger language for fire
• Clarify authority with application review, permitting, inspections, post-accident review, and decommissioning.
• Strengthen Road Use Agreements for duration of project construction, as well as post-construction.
• Add requirements for applicants to consult with municipalities/tribal entities within five (5) miles of proposed project
boundaries.
• Codify a mandate of the use of best available, commercially proven technology to minimize wildlife impacts.
• Codify Mandate for site studies such as environmental, cultural, wetlands, and photo-simulations.
22TXT-A 25-001

<!-- page 1253 -->
PROPOSED UPDATES TO ORDINANCE (WIND SPECIFIC)
• Waivers can be accepted from nonparticipating, adjoining properties within required setback boundaries.
• Waivers are specific to wind setbacks.
23TXT-A 25-001

<!-- page 1254 -->
PROPOSED UPDATES TO ORDINANCE (SOLAR SPECIFIC)
• Setbacks and development standards must comply with zoning district in which facility is located.
• Waivers can be accepted from non-participating, adjoining properties within required setback boundaries.
• Waivers are specific to solar setbacks.
• Added provision for screening adjacent to residential developments.
